conditions: This is the source's strong opinion about naming, drawn from pre-internet advertising; modern search and logo-led brands sometimes succeed with coined or short names, but the memory argument still favors pronounceable, meaningful names for new entries.
Initials can be useful in domains or handles for consistency; the trap concerns using them as the primary brand expression.

9e3ddfa5cf560f797a2bb23d.applies_when: Choosing a brand name for a genuinely new product category, new store concept or novel private label, rather than a new SKU in an existing category.
conditions: The source's rule is strict: coined names are only sanctioned for first-in-mind novel products. Applying them to ordinary new SKUs is the failure mode this rule guards against.
Category-first status can be lost; the coined-name advantage is not permanent.

e192263b85cc676c7aa70c03.applies_when: Deciding brand architecture for a line extension: whether a new SKU, category or sub-brand should carry the house brand or a separate name.
conditions: These are the source's rules of thumb, not formulas with numeric thresholds; the source gives no benchmark scores or weights.
Rules interact: high volume can still be overridden by weak significance and low ad support, so use judgement.

ad5c24b3c95342018b0280f2.applies_when: Planning catalog expansion, adding a new category under an existing store brand, or evaluating a tempting free-ride addition.
conditions: The source's position is strongly anti-line-extension; modern retailers and marketplaces often extend successfully, so treat it as a warning about dilution risk rather than an absolute prohibition.
Dilution is slow and hard to measure directly; the shopping-list test is a qualitative check, not a metric.

1aaf6ab34b2e66e32595f55a.applies_when: Reviewing whether a store brand should own multiple categories, or during a product roadmap review before approving a stretch SKU.
conditions: The principle is a heuristic about perception, not a measured effect; the source offers no numeric threshold for how different is 'too different.'
Real companies do stretch brands successfully; the principle predicts pressure on meaning, not certain failure.

6b22f8028e7076e7c5816535.applies_when: Diagnosing whether a store brand is losing meaning, or screening a proposed extension before it further dilutes the name.
conditions: This is a qualitative test drawn from the source, not a benchmarked metric; pass/fail depends on how customers actually talk about the category.
Brands built on lifestyle or identity, rather than category, may not be expected to substitute for a category noun; interpret the test in that light.

3bdfbcd79086d0fe67c784c0.applies_when: Validating a new store or product name, or measuring whether current branding has actually lodged a category association.
conditions: The source uses an informal, illustrative test; it is not a rigorous research method and should be treated as a directional signal.
Name recall is one component of positioning; a name can recall the category yet still lose on other rungs.

94ce0d0c21b6934182e7e029.applies_when: You're setting or auditing your store's overall brand direction before a range review, rebrand, or category expansion.
conditions: Kotler's foreword presents positioning as preceding the 4Ps; the authors' own framing is more extreme. Treat both as frameworks, not measurement instructions.
The examples (Volvo, Häagen-Dazs, L'eggs, Little Caesars) are historical illustrations, not benchmarks or promises for your store.

1a89c8f731f56e25ef60dcbe.applies_when: You're choosing which new product, category, or niche to launch or how to frame your store's claim.
conditions: The authors' claim that 'second is nowhere' is their strong opinion. Many categories have viable number-two and number-three players.
Being first in the mind is a hypothesis about perception; the book offers anecdote, not measurement methods. Test your own category with real shoppers before committing.

d6bb004cc9ea61609a6119d3.applies_when: You're writing a positioning brief, planning a relaunch, or deciding how to differentiate on PDP copy and acquisition creative.
conditions: Seven is described as the common limit from Harvard psychologist George A. Miller's work; treat it as a heuristic for how many brands people recall, not a precise per-category constant.
Ladder position is perception; verify with several respondent groups before redesigning your whole brand around one survey.

0d6ad2f3cdfc0731f686523f.applies_when: You're a number-two or later entrant in an established category and need a differentiation strategy for your homepage, PDP, and ad creative.
conditions: The Avis profit figures in the book ($1.2M, $2.6M, $5M over successive years) are a historical case example, not a forecast for comparative positioning.
Comparative advertising rules and platform policies vary by country and change over time — verify current requirements before publishing.

92e5149e81d9fc79c1f46fc6.applies_when: You're launching a novel product, format, or bundle and need PDP and landing-page framing that makes it instantly understandable.
conditions: The book offers this as a communication principle with anecdotal support, not a tested checklist. Validate comprehension with real shoppers before scaling media spend.
If the 'what it isn't' frame implies an unverified comparison claim (e.g., against a health or safety standard), check regulatory and advertising constraints.

079c0cc5fa06950033c13a1c.applies_when: You're deciding what goes on a homepage hero, PDP first screen, or acquisition ad when you have many possible claims.
conditions: The authors' claim that mind-changing is 'the road to advertising disaster' is a strong opinion; repositioning campaigns do sometimes work over long horizons and large budgets.
'Oversimplify' can conflict with legal, safety, or efficacy disclosure duties — simplify the persuasive layer, not required information.

482e1229432994c711ca255e.applies_when: You're writing PDP copy, product names, or ad creative for a product whose quality or taste/effect is judged subjectively.
conditions: The Gallo/Burgundy anecdote and the Gablinger's example are illustrative, not controlled experiments, and results are not guaranteed for your product.
Raising expectations without delivering can damage repeat purchase and reviews — the principle assumes the product can perform as expected.

db70929c9e071d8a6cbe6d98.applies_when: You sell a commodity or undifferentiated product and need a claim that changes how shoppers categorize you without changing the product.
conditions: Retail price and search placement mechanics differ from radio ads, so treat the Michelob and Miller outcomes as category-education examples, not ecommerce benchmarks.
Perspective repositioning works only where the attribute is defensible; if everyone already claims it, the move is not available.

6c5720ed9b21396f4e0ba378.applies_when: You're an unranked or number-two store in a category and need honest, differentiated messaging that feels credible to shoppers.
conditions: The book gives no measurement method for establishing 'rank in the mind'; use your own recall surveys cautiously.
Avis's turnaround came alongside many operational factors the book does not isolate — do not attribute revenue outcomes to the admission alone.

4fc88b60ad480b78226fcaa1.applies_when: You're evaluating whether a brand name has become diluted before extending it to a new product line or category.
conditions: 'Shopping-list test' is described as a conceptual check; the source does not specify sample size, scoring, or a pass/fail threshold.
Generic naming is sometimes a deliberate strategy (Kleenex, Xerox) — dilution risk is not automatically a failure.

4f6df01afd17c1af8a7c2920.applies_when: You're planning a product line extension or new category entry and must decide whether to reuse your existing brand name or create a new one.
conditions: The source presents these as guiding questions, not a formula with numeric cut-offs; scoring is judgment-based.
The claim that line extension 'seldom works' is a strong opinion from the authors and is contested in practice; treat it as the source's stated position.

e2d2e2bdb4c664cb4ca4d2fb.applies_when: You're adding a SKU, flavor, size, or adjacent category to an existing brand and want the extension to strengthen rather than dilute the parent.
conditions: The book's LifeSavers gum example is about a specific failed free-ride case, not a general prohibition on parent-brand endorsement of extensions.
The book also allows that line extension can work (GE cited); this card states the conditions said to favor it, not an absolute rule.

46df3117bf9a3ac4930e3678.applies_when: You're deciding whether to put an existing store or brand name on an adjacent product range, and want to anticipate where the name stops helping.
conditions: The book's position is a strong one, presented through a single case example; results vary by category and are not guaranteed in either direction.
The book itself names exceptions where line extension can work (GE), so treat the free-ride trap as a warning, not a universal law.

69570ad504f4e49dc22a920d.applies_when: You're considering putting an existing brand name on a second, genuinely different product and need to assess the risk to both.
conditions: The teeter-totter principle is described at the level of a marketing principle, not a tested model; no quantification of the trade-off is provided.
'Distinctly different' is undefined in the source; classify using your own category and customer research.

e247ee27ad80dc32e7426a42.applies_when: You're kicking off a positioning or rebrand effort and need a starting checklist before spending on channels.
conditions: The book names the six questions but the source excerpt describes Chapter 24 rather than listing them verbatim; treat the phrasing as a faithful reconstruction of the intent, not a quotation.
Validate with real shoppers before investing; the checklist structures judgment rather than replacing research.

78b60e028cb628b64f83c011.applies_when: You're setting up an ongoing positioning program and need the operating mindset that keeps it consistent across launches and campaigns.
conditions: These are prescriptions about stance and character, not measurable procedures; they complement but do not replace testing.
The source frames this largely through advertising, so adapt the mindset to catalog, packaging, and site copy rather than only paid channels.

a7054e16df6cb17ef4268934.applies_when: You're planning launch timing and audience selection for a new product or campaign.
conditions: The book argues segmentation and narrow targeting are more effective than broad reach; this is a stated principle rather than a controlled finding.
The phrase 'window in the mind' is the authors' metaphor, not a scheduling rule.

0435c01adf0bb1759932751b.applies_when: You're reviewing your acquisition creative and deciding whether to lead with features, brand imagery, or a positioning claim.
conditions: The eras are the authors' historical narrative, not an empirical study; treat them as framing devices.
Copying a competitor's supposed era position is not the point — the shift is about strategy orientation, not a new ad template.

ff2d9fce9f885510166869db.applies_when: Choosing positioning for a store or brand entering a category where a dominant competitor already owns the top rung in customer minds (e.g., a new gear shop vs. an established giant).
conditions: The No. 2 strategy requires an actual recognized leader; if the category has no clear leader, the relationship has no anchor.
This is a positioning frame, not proof of sales results — case figures cited come from the source's historical examples, not your market.

7cbf151d9951531fb508dfaa.applies_when: Deciding what new product, size, or category to launch or how to angle a product-page headline for a crowded category.
conditions: The source notes few truly empty positions remain today; many categories require repositioning a competitor instead.
A technical achievement or genuinely new product feature can still fail if no mental slot exists for it (the Frost 8/80 'dry white whisky' example).

7f129dfe890c89b5bc79bd38.applies_when: Setting price tier strategy or writing pricing-related copy for a product line or category page.
conditions: The source explicitly warns that charging high prices is not itself the way to get rich — greed is not positioning.
A high price without a position, product story, and receptive category will drive customers away.
Retailer discount emphasis can erase low-price opportunities over time (the source's generic-brand point).

326a3dca9341c8c6cbd452f0.applies_when: Entering a saturated category where all obvious positions are taken and you need a wedge for your brand story or comparison content.
conditions: The source acknowledges repositioning draws ethical complaints, though it argues comparative advertising is legal and can be done honestly and fairly.
Repositioning can backfire if your own product has an unclear name or weak follow-through — Scope's repositioning of Listerine was undercut by an unmouthwash-like name.
Once a product is mentally tagged a loser, the source says recovery is very hard — repositioning works best as an offensive move, not a rescue.

e8ed01410f31b8048c62bb2d.applies_when: Writing brand messaging or category pages when your store genuinely owns the leading mental position in a niche.
conditions: Leaders should not read their own ads too admiringly; the source urges covering new developments by adopting promising innovations early or with a multibrand launch.
Ignore-competition messaging assumes genuine category leadership in the customer's mind, not self-declared metrics like 'best-selling above $1,000 east of the Mississippi.'

be7172025ae3ad1ce9bab497.applies_when: Deciding whether to launch a new sub-brand, product line, or SKU versus attaching a new variant to your best-selling brand.
conditions: This is a strategy for brands that already own a strong position; the source warns a follower copying the leader is a 'me-too' move, not covering.
Internal resistance is common — management often sees the new product as a competitor rather than protection, so the covering move is hard to sell internally.

a3b068db34cdc3d4b13ae8ee.applies_when: Reviewing brand messaging, campaign themes, or homepage copy that has accumulated multiple taglines over time.
conditions: The source treats consistency as the core positioning discipline; it doesn't argue you can never launch new products, only that the owned position shouldn't be abandoned.
Failing to hold your position risks being passed by a competitor, as the source warns about Avis and National.

d68f5389fbe9fd8aa4f252f6.applies_when: Deciding whether to enter a new product category, compete with a dominant platform, or fund an aggressive growth goal.
conditions: The RCA and GE computer outcomes are historical case examples, not predictions about your market; treat them as illustrations of a rule about head-on competition.
The source also says extra effort is valuable when applied early to establish leadership — timing matters, so 'can't get there' applies mainly to late, head-on moves.

32142fdf58930bd258189588.applies_when: Writing category, homepage, or brand copy and choosing whether to keep broad, inclusive messaging or commit to a defined customer segment.
conditions: This is the source's advice for brands trying to build a position; it concedes a broad, already-dominant brand may survive without a sharp niche.
The source's argument rests on the overcommunicated-market premise, not on measured conversion data.

526980d48d67a0d8efc50dea.applies_when: Naming a new product, private label, or sub-brand, or diagnosing why a well-positioned offer underperforms.
conditions: The naming failures cited (Scope, Max Factor's 'Just Call Me Maxi') are historical anecdotes presented as illustrations, not controlled evidence.
The source treats the name as critical but does not claim a name alone fixes a product with no position.

c548656c431cf6ee64df4085.applies_when: Planning a product or category launch, deciding launch timing, naming, and marketing spend against an incumbent.
conditions: The source's claim about 'first gets twice the long-term share' is presented as a general historical pattern, not a formula or a guaranteed benchmark for your category.
This reflects the source's view that first-mover advantage dominates; a truly differentiated late entry can still win, but not by fighting the leader head-on.

266a692c2863030a1bdd1141.applies_when: Writing product page copy, ingredient lists, or label descriptions for food, supplements, or any product judged by sensory quality.
conditions: The Pringle's outcome is a historical case, not a controlled test; use as illustration, not a guaranteed result.
Once a product is widely perceived as a 'loser,' the source says recovering is very hard, so this lever works better ahead of negative perception than after.

a57fe56ea376d37a21937b1e.applies_when: Planning comparison content, 'us vs. them' pages, or competitor-focused acquisition creative.
conditions: Repositioning draws ethical objections, which the source acknowledges while defending it as more effective than brag-and-boast.
Comparative claims carry legal and platform risk; the source's regulatory timeline is historical and specific rules should be verified with counsel.

206ed18a889e7dd387414098.applies_when: Timing a promotional push or brand investment in a category where you're roughly tied with a rival for the top spot.
conditions: These patterns come from historical consumer-goods and auto examples; the source presents them as general positioning rules, not modern measured benchmarks.
The 'twice the long-term share' figure is a source heuristics claim, not a calculation to plan against literally.

6eae715aafa428f4e0ebbdc4.applies_when: Choosing an angle for a new product, line, or landing-page narrative in a mature category where broad claims are taken.
conditions: Numeric share claims like Aim's '10 percent of the toothpaste market' are historical examples, not targets.
The source's timing claims are anecdotal case comparisons, not controlled tests, so validate demand for the dimension with customers before building around it.

46a0f217dd381841fa7d4c3f.applies_when: Naming a new product, brand, SKU or storefront, or deciding whether to rename an existing product line.
conditions: The source is opinionated and dated; the core claim is a positioning argument, not a measured benchmark.
Benefit-led names risk becoming generic if too close to the category (see separate card on that trap).

b17d31320962c2276520ad6d.applies_when: Deciding between a descriptive name (e.g. Soy Butter, Spray 'n Wash) and a coined or abstract brand name for a new product or store line.
conditions: The source's claim that only first-movers can afford coined names is a heuristic, not a tested rule.
Descriptive names invite trademark trouble and category substitution (Lite problem).

5fffd494c3af50fc9a360416.applies_when: Naming or trademarking a launch SKU, deciding whether to coin a new word for a new product format, or reviewing a product name that has become a category catch-all.
conditions: Choice of name is a trade-off: too abstract and the prospect learns nothing; too descriptive and you lose the mark.
Legal standards vary by jurisdiction and category; get current local advice.

86ea8f99ebefcb77a7587381.applies_when: Portfolio review: assessing whether a legacy brand or product name still communicates the current offer, or whether a rename is warranted.
conditions: Rename case studies are retrospective examples, not guarantees of improved sales.
Goodrich opted to keep the name and effectively told customers it was their problem to remember it — a defensible but expensive choice.

7bd3e22840b8a137fdc749c4.applies_when: Choosing a store or product name, writing ad headlines or slogans, or preparing a brand name for voice search and audio advertising.
conditions: Phonetic shorthand rules were developed in an era dominated by radio and print; streaming and app search change the retrieval rules but not the value of a pronounceable name.

dca1b04ea88b10fa605de960.applies_when: Deciding whether to brand a new store line, private label or acquisition sub-brand with initials or an acronym, or reviewing a corporate rebrand.
conditions: The 49%/68% awareness survey is a single source study and should be read as illustrative, not a benchmark for your category.
Some acronyms are deliberate and work as names (CARE, MADD, Fiat, Sabena), so the rule is 'do the initials add phonetic or mnemonic value?' not 'never abbreviate'.

ecf11f686ff7a27d31e6d3c1.applies_when: Deciding whether to launch a new product or category under the existing hero brand name versus creating a new brand or sub-brand, e.g. an existing supplement brand moving into skincare.
conditions: The source argues that Procter & Gamble's no-house-name strategy beat Colgate-Palmolive (roughly twice the business and five times the profit) — a historical comparison, not a guaranteed operating rule.
There are exceptions: some brands extend successfully when the new product is genuinely within the same ladder. Run a name-fit test before launching.

dbea05de1e298d4a4fea6f0b.applies_when: Naming a flagship SKU or private-label item where you want one benefit to be remembered, e.g. an extended-life battery, a durability claim, or a specific food benefit.
conditions: Sears' retail-connection problem is real; a great name cannot fix distribution customers cannot easily reach.

3dc57a790b44752be812e919.applies_when: Launching a new product line in a new category under a company that already owns a position in another category.
conditions: This is the source's opinion, illustrated through historical cases; not every extension fails.
Sub-brand naming can capture some, but not all, of the separation benefits described.

9eb8f61cd2ab8eb7b5806b9b.applies_when: Naming or renaming a product whose origin or formulation is unfamiliar to buyers — alternative ingredients, plant-based or lab-made goods, or a product seen as an imitation.
conditions: Renaming an entrenched concept early — before the powerful name takes root — is much more effective than late; the source notes 'price maintenance' as a blocking strategy would probably have worked only early.
Some origin words carry stigma the brand may not be able to neutralize; validate with real customer language before committing.

018fc1cec3a22f4365c38396.applies_when: Portfolio and pricing decisions when a hero brand or hero SKU is being considered as a vehicle for a new offer, bundle or adjacent category.
conditions: The source is strongly anti-extension; some brands do extend profitably, so treat this as a risk framework rather than an absolute ban.

a8f3bf799a4e090bcbca278e.applies_when: Planning a PR push, press outreach or influencer campaign for a new store, brand or hero product, and deciding when to use your best story.
conditions: The source treats publicity as finite, which may understate the compounding effect of a well-run content channel.

ee3bccb269e022a20c9204a4.applies_when: Deciding whether an acquired brand or a newly developed product should carry the parent store/brand name, after an acquisition or a category expansion.
conditions: The source's naming analysis is drawn from large industrial and packaged-goods history; small ecommerce portfolios may have different trade-offs.

defb93a8527020b136e46613.applies_when: Renaming a store, a legacy product line, or a brand after a pivot, product obsolescence or a merger.
conditions: Renaming is rare in practice because companies believe they have too much equity in the current name; the source counter-cites Olin, Mobil, Uniroyal, Xerox and Exxon as companies that made the change work.

c4a8fdae883ca1b301a45699.applies_when: Deciding whether to launch a new product category, sub-brand, or SKU under your existing store/brand name, or evaluating whether an existing catalog is already diluted.
conditions: The source is a 1980s packaged-goods argument; its share-loss examples are illustrative, not benchmarks for your store.
A broad house name works fine for low-involvement commodity items where shoppers have no going-in preference — the test matters most where you want to own a category.

3c603945dca9ef67099e4e14.applies_when: Interpreting early sales data after launching a new SKU under an existing brand name, or setting expectations with a founder before a sub-brand launch.
conditions: The '$35 per supermarket' figure is the source's illustrative arithmetic for physical retail distribution, not a benchmark for ecommerce.
Anti-extension argument, not a blanket ban; the source explicitly allows extension when there is no competition and no intention to build a position.

322fbe17b694f5b2a5763339.applies_when: Considering whether to attach your main brand name to an adjacent product line, ingredient variant, or differently-positioned version.
conditions: Share figures are historical packaged-goods examples from the source, not predictive benchmarks.
The source also warns the decline is 'bound to continue' — an opinion about trajectory, worth testing rather than assuming.

3ca345f68121e6cfbf0a8a97.applies_when: Looking for growth from an existing hero product without launching a new SKU, or planning messaging and landing-page angles for a narrowly perceived product.
conditions: Source's examples are beverages and personal care; the mechanism (usage broadening) transfers, the results do not.
Advertising-intensive: the source ties these wins to sustained promotion, so a silent PDP edit alone is unlikely to shift perception.

03327dab7ce51ef51dfdafbb.applies_when: Deciding whether a premium tier or a cheaper entry model should carry your existing brand name, and how to name tiers in a catalog or subscription ladder.
conditions: The step-up and step-down patterns are the source's observations from liquor and autos, stated as tendencies, not laws.
The Vaseline case shows extension can survive when the extension name is what people actually say — verify this through customer language, not internal naming documents.

4e20426232bb64bb73fb16c8.applies_when: Deciding naming and brand architecture for a new product launch, collection, or private-label item in a multi-product catalog.
conditions: These are the source's stated heuristics, framed as 'an economics call as much as a judgment call' — apply with your own volume and margin data.
The rules assume a world where advertising budget and distribution channel differ by product; re-derive them for your channel mix.

8a909a51fd898428f27e5648.applies_when: You are early into a new product category, format, or claim and choosing how to name and describe it in your store and ads.
conditions: All share figures are the source's historical examples, not forecasts for your category.
The source acknowledges that leading brands like Marlboro and Winston also extended — it frames the outcome as a tendency, not an inevitability.

c3e977f3ebfa33eb3cc17bef.applies_when: Reviewing an expanding product line or variant count, or planning a range extension for a category-leading product.
conditions: The Volkswagen decline is the source's example, with its own era's competitive context, not a general law about range width.
Range breadth can be right for some retailers; the source's argument targets brands attempting to own a position in the customer's mind.

779fc1b761d8ca34cfd19926.applies_when: Deciding how many product categories one brand name should cover, versus launching a separate brand or holding a category-specific name.
conditions: Del Monte and Dole conclusions are the source's market observations, not universal rules.
The source explicitly tolerates broad names for commodities with no meaningful brand preference.

6b536db78f7b5b53a528bb19.applies_when: Reviewing whether a category-leading SKU in your catalog actually owns a distinct claim, or launching an innovation that looks like a variant of an existing product.
conditions: History is the source's packaged-goods examples, not a measured forecast.
The lesson is about distinct position, not merely renaming: a rename without a real, communicated difference will not carry the position.

6b46650fd04c67f1d8028d1c.applies_when: Marketing a marketplace, region, or store category where demand must be grown before your own product can sell, including multi-seller marketplace or regional seller positioning.
conditions: The Belgium program, per the source, was not ultimately executed because new management did not commit — the source treats that as its own lesson about long-term commitment.
This is an agency case from the source's era; the transferable mechanism is anchoring to existing perceptions, not the specific media plan.

ea573c35f69c92249e71dff9.applies_when: Planning ad creative, PDP imagery, or a landing-page hero where your category's visuals look identical to competitors'.
conditions: The Bermuda visual is cited as effective and long-running, not as a measured lift.
The Belgium television work is described by the source as generating substantial response, but the program was not fully deployed — treat response as directional.

f0d81e00c9a55aef8eef36b1.applies_when: Setting positioning or rebranding direction for a store and deciding how to protect it through team, agency, or platform changes.
conditions: The source's evidence is a case study where the program was abandoned; it demonstrates the risk, not a measured effect of commitment.
The source acknowledges this is difficult in a constantly changing political environment — the same applies to fast-changing platform and marketing environments.

97bafe17846bfa7fbe771de2.applies_when: Deciding which adjacent category, product line, or feature set to enter when your store already owns one strong position and a bigger competitor owns the adjacent one.
conditions: Xerox's attempts are recounted as failures by the source; this is a strategic proposal made at the time, not a documented success.
The leg framework reflects that era's office market; the reasoning about avoiding the leader's turf transfers, the specific technologies do not.

dc9410d03a81c7a42d5ecb80.applies_when: Positioning your store or company as a whole — for recruiting, supplier relationships, or investor conversations— rather than positioning one product.
conditions: These are the source's observations about corporate advertising platforms, offered as strong opinions ('diversification is not the answer').
The Pullman and Greyhound examples are historical; verify current brand facts before citing them.

2362e3449185aa8afe1f00d9.applies_when: Planning brand photography, a category hero image, or creative territory for a store whose category visuals are interchangeable with competitors'.
conditions: The Jamaica passage is where the source's extract ends; the resolution of that search is not stated here.
The insight is about search method (existing perception first), not proof that new photography can never work.

7a5f6e23a28dcc13fb520626.applies_when: Deciding brand positioning for a store, destination, or product when you are tempted to shoot new creative or write new copy about your own features.
conditions: Borrowing another destination's imagery risks looking derivative if the analogy is not backed by verifiable substance.
The source attributes Jamaica's inaction to politics, not positioning failure — execution depends on decision-makers, not the strategy alone.

babb616ba8a918fd717183cf.applies_when: Choosing positioning for a slow-moving SKU or category where your brand has little advertising budget and competitors dominate the mental category.
conditions: The Milk Duds sales result (reverse of a downward trend, record volume) is a case example, not a promised outcome.
Self-cannibalization objections may be raised by internal teams, as with Mailgram; expect to defend the strategic logic.

9794ccdb926ce12b587b0b87.applies_when: Introducing a new service or subscription tier and deciding which existing behavior or alternative to contrast it against in messaging.
conditions: Awareness and volume figures are a specific test-market case, not a benchmark for other services.
The source says the company later switched strategy to 'next-day delivery' and volume declined — an example, not proof that strategy changes always cause decline.

fcfff9855adc5037bab95851.applies_when: Choosing a positioning territory for a local retailer, bank, or store facing larger outside competitors, when internal consensus is weak.
conditions: The source says formal research is often not needed when the insight is intuitive (Western Union/Telegram), but it is useful for building strategy and selling it to top management.
Perception shifts in research do not guarantee real-world branch or financial results.

6355cdae1a6b79393b2e98b4.applies_when: Positioning a smaller store or local brand against a large national competitor whose weakness is slowness or bureaucracy.
conditions: The reported earnings increase of $30 million (26%) is a specific case result, not a general expectation.
The source's essence criterion is that a good position transcends every aspect of the company — if operations can't match the ad, the strategy fails.

2e309f07feea6f476a03e009.applies_when: Selling a product or store that is farther, pricier, or less convenient than alternatives and needs a reason the customer will accept.

b75dfff1cc41042058abda7c.applies_when: Deciding where to concentrate brand and PR effort, and how to measure community reach versus raw audience size.
conditions: The 1,500–3,000 figures are the author's heuristics, not computed audience benchmarks.

894eb8e3217061b40def0141.applies_when: Planning category entry, product-market expansion or launch sequencing when early-adopter traction has not converted into mainstream sales.
conditions: The source frames this as Moore's chasm applied to marketing generally; specifics about which stores can bridge it are your application, not documented results.

bc48055c28eabff4505465bb.applies_when: Seeding a product in a specific community, campus, niche or region before attempting broader rollout.
conditions: Facebook's and WHI's outcomes are case illustrations; the author also warns that the final leap to a huge mass market is unlikely for most marketers.

2b78cfe849b3ba8a2bb15dd4.applies_when: Choosing product selection strategy, niche assortment breadth, or deciding whether to compete as a tiny seller on a giant marketplace.
conditions: The Amazon halves and T-shirt volume are the source's illustrative numbers, not audited data.

9db7234804f893854440ca97.applies_when: Designing a user-generated, community, referral or affiliate program and setting realistic time-to-traction expectations.
conditions: This is the author's own failed venture, presented as a lesson; the causes are his diagnosis, not an independently verified post-mortem.

6f6fc2d540e9fdcafec7cbc9.applies_when: Setting realistic expectations for a content-to-conversion funnel and deciding which stage to improve.
conditions: These are the author's approximate, single-observation numbers from one creator at one time, explicitly 'your mileage may vary,' and are not benchmarks for stores.

f876adc459c2976a9b4d8fb1.applies_when: Launching an unfamiliar product or replenishment habit where mainstream shoppers need peer reassurance.
conditions: The source case concerns water adoption in a village, not a measured online-store conversion experiment.
Visibility and conversation do not establish incrementality; price, access and product usefulness also affect adoption.

1d9f9a55d0305b59b00a354b.applies_when: Writing an About page, launch email or founder-led product video.
conditions: This applies the source narrative framework to store content; the source does not establish a conversion uplift.
Do not manufacture urgency, vulnerability or customer outcomes.

47bed4781dc35caa3a46adbb.applies_when: Designing a brand community for products connected to a shared hobby, practice or identity.
conditions: Community participation is not automatically profitable retention; evaluate the store outcome separately.
Avoid hostile in-group messaging or manipulation to manufacture belonging.

2bf198a5792e8fe747d4e4e9.applies_when: Planning ownership and cadence for a store community, loyalty program or customer education series.
conditions: The source describes activity decay metaphorically as a half-life; it does not provide a measurable universal decay rate.
Do not assume engagement proves repeat-purchase impact.

0198511845bbce8468a06516.applies_when: A product attracts early adopters but struggles to reach more cautious shoppers.
conditions: Adapted from the source account of repeated local cookware demonstrations; no fixed online conversion frequency is established.

1fe8a3dca718451c6992a509.applies_when: Launching a premium replacement or upgrade in a mature product category.
conditions: The source uses early Tesla positioning as a historical illustration; its claims are not current specifications or ecommerce performance evidence.
Avoid unsupported superiority claims or shaming customers for owning an alternative.

f7af8c4da42443c263b60da4.applies_when: Deciding whether a product page or brand launch is ready for a limited initial release.
conditions: This applies the source good-enough-then-better principle; it is not permission to skip product safety, accurate claims or working transactions.
A weak response may reflect demand, audience or offer problems, not merely design polish.

5594f9ad6d2bb87104fe6936.applies_when: Reviewing a campaign or product-page promise that could raise short-term conversion while harming trust.
conditions: This is an ecommerce application of the source argument about marketer responsibility, not a quantified growth tactic.

9d81ed21b34287793607a3d1.applies_when: Choosing which new product, bundle concept, or brand name to take forward from a shortlist of candidates.
conditions: Polarization is a signal of distinctiveness, not proof of commercial viability; a name or product can be polarizing for the wrong reason (confusing, offensive, hard to say).
This is a decision heuristic from the source's creative-naming experience, not a measured conversion benchmark.

ae16dc1d542abb716075ee68.applies_when: Running a brainstorm for a product launch, seasonal campaign, bundle concept or PDP angle where early criticism keeps killing options.
conditions: Suspending evaluation is an ideation-phase rule, not a license to skip feasibility, margin or compliance review before launch.
Someone still has to run the evaluation pass; deferring judgment indefinitely stalls decisions.

7fec0334bcfe1bdf471e17c6.applies_when: Designing a team or customer ideation session for new products, offers, campaigns or merchandising concepts.
conditions: Approximate ideas still need a real evaluation and feasibility pass; the framework delays judgement, it does not replace it.
If the team only ever produces safe ideas, the spectrum instruction is not working and the framing may need to be re-set.

24a1ee273847a825f1906899.applies_when: Deciding how much effort and budget to put into naming an ecommerce brand, product line or sub-brand before launch instead of accepting a Friday-afternoon placeholder name.
conditions: Name advantage is stated as most influential in the launch window; after that, marketplace dynamics take over.
Source is a naming-agency creative director speaking from his portfolio; no independent attribution data is presented.

0c6615eb40297c62c927f978.applies_when: Naming a new product, sub-brand or storefront when the category is full of descriptive names (fiber, mop, natural, fresh) and you need a defensible direction rather than a list of words.
conditions: You may return to a rejected direction once the product truth is clearer; the first hypothesis is a starting filter, not a verdict.
For ordinary commodity products without a breakthrough feature, the differentiation often has to come from the benefit framing rather than a unique ingredient.

6286b8c570e97c3990a533dd.applies_when: Writing PDP hero copy, naming a new SKU, or repositioning a supplement, food or personal-care product where every competitor's label says the same category word.
conditions: The Feather example is an in-conversation thought exercise, not a launched brand with results.
Forcing an abstract benefit name onto a highly search-driven commodity category can hurt discoverability unless the category term stays visible in titles and tags.

3b6889a898c9ee8388a16ecf.applies_when: Running any divergent naming, campaign or creative sprint for a store, SKU or ad concept and tempted to converge after the first hundred ideas.
conditions: 2,000 is the source agency's working number for a paid naming engagement, not a required target for every creative task.
Volume without an explicit selection framework just produces a longer unusable list.

8d9104bffa0d00e4cacac5b9.applies_when: Structuring an internal or agency naming/creative sprint for a new brand, SKU or campaign and deciding how many people should work on it and with what information.
conditions: The 18-month internal study is the source's private research; methodology is described as 'a little sloppy and crude' by his own account.
Two-person teams assume availability; solo operators should substitute sequential briefs, not skip the diversity of framing.

4e009c4e7883c8b568859193.applies_when: Filling the candidate pool for a new brand or product name when the obvious descriptive options are taken or legally blocked.
conditions: Databases are a starting point, not a source of finished names; raw output needs heavy filtering.
Watch for trademark collisions — the source routes shortlists through paralegals and trademark attorneys before presentation.

d9c1184d1dd67ca7f5b41c2c.applies_when: Sitting down to generate names or headline options yourself for a product, bundle or campaign and needing to get into flow quickly.
conditions: This routine reflects one practitioner's working method, not a validated protocol.
Using AI for context rather than name generation is the source's stated approach; his competitive claim now rests on judging names from proprietary data.

69fd0d7859ecdd0cb5edc1a3.applies_when: Reviewing creative submissions from staff or agencies — naming options, ad concepts, PDP concepts — and catching yourself about to kill an idea in the room.
conditions: Permission to speculate does not remove eventual client or business evaluation; the source explicitly says people still have to do the right thing for clients.
Soft language only works if the underlying idea later gets a genuine decision — constant deferral stalls the project.

0db63ae1d97cb4501143676f.applies_when: Deciding between a safe, easily-approved brand name, campaign concept or offer angle and a polarizing one that some of your team dislikes.
conditions: Polarization is a signal of energy, not proof of quality — the source says you may not decide to use it.
Believability at first glance is a stated agency rule, not a published benchmark.

b7494c09d18d569fdc235b29.applies_when: Presenting name or brand options to founders, retailers or internal stakeholders who rarely make creative decisions and are choosing between unfamiliar candidates.
conditions: Context presentation influences perception and can sway stakeholders — it is a decision aid, not consumer evidence.
Mock-ups must not imply real coverage or real endorsements that do not exist.

99647fecb304f2a29c7c11fe.applies_when: Choosing between shortlisted names for a brand, collection or product line and needing a consistent scoring rationale rather than gut preference.
conditions: The 1-10 scores are the source's subjective creative judgment, made without knowing the companies.
Sound-symbolism claims are presented as the agency's accumulated research; they are directional, not guarantees of consumer response.
The naming mechanics of specific sound symbolism belong to brand-creative work rather than store operations.

fa435f935bc214d3c9ea6c07.applies_when: Deciding whether to change a store, product line or brand name that creates friction in search, spelling or customer recall, and planning the relaunch.
conditions: The 'never seen equity loss' claim is the source's agency experience, not independent research.
Consumer-goods giants with decades of brand equity are explicitly excluded from the easy-rename advice.
Renaming carries real SEO, marketplace-listing and repeat-purchase risk that the source does not quantify.

14751ff10cd0b6824ccae8b9.applies_when: Setting up the brief for naming, positioning or a major PDP rewrite, or diagnosing why your creative output keeps landing in the invisible zone.
conditions: The full agency process takes weeks and multiple people; small operators must compress it without skipping the sequencing.
Timing bands such as two cycles in two and a half weeks assume team members working several projects at once.

a68351f8218dd3830cee07d6.applies_when: Founders or operators trying to scale creative output beyond themselves for naming, ad creative, PDP copy or content.
conditions: These are the source's management prescriptions and personal practice, not measured team-performance results.
Small teams may not be able to isolate phases in separate people; they still need to isolate them in time.

3cd4209d8e570b07aa4ced9c.applies_when: A headline, PDP narrative, campaign angle or product story feels like generic category copy and you need a genuinely different perspective.
conditions: The 30% hit rate is the source's own estimate from practice.
Borrowed metaphors must be checked against what your product actually does before use in claims.

0b1a266ee4fda0ba67b61ce8.applies_when: When naming a new product, brand line, or store, or when you have a longlist of candidates and need to pick the one to launch with.
conditions: The source runs a naming firm whose competitive advantage is proprietary data and software integrated with AI; a small brand will not replicate that dataset, so allocate more weight to your own category and customer knowledge.

a714872495eec9ea5bf8a0ba.applies_when: When planning budget, scope, or an in-house vs agency decision for a new brand, product line, or flagship SKU.
conditions: These are one firm's 2026-era numbers for consulting projects; costs vary widely by region, scope and firm size.
Small ecommerce brands rarely need this spend for every SKU; reserve it for the flagship or umbrella brand.

d08af5a4ebfa18870caf5bc9.applies_when: When you have just launched or rebranded and want to know whether the new name is gaining traction before locking in packaging, listings and ad spend.
conditions: The source describes the practice but gives no numeric thresholds; choose your own meaningful improvement level.
Small samples can be noisy, so treat the second wave as directional.

15f3c7de96221b14f6cedbf3.applies_when: When briefing your team or an agency on ad creative, product naming, landing-page concepts, or any ideation session where output has become predictable.
conditions: This is the source's own coaching device for creative teams, not a documented experiment; expect to sift a lot of unusable material.
Not every category can absorb a bizarre concept, and in regulated categories legal review still applies.

bcf9030294059313e287056d.applies_when: When deciding how far to automate naming, product-copy generation, or creative concepts, and what capability to keep human.
conditions: The 16-month integration and the project mix are one firm's experience, not a productivity benchmark.
AI output may reproduce existing or trademarked names; run clearance checks before committing to anything.

bcee1e69de7698ae45475b5d.applies_when: Weekly planning for a lean ecommerce team or solo operator overwhelmed by merchandising, marketing, and ops tasks.
conditions: Source is the presenter's personal operating rule, not a proven system for all teams.
Some urgent ops issues (stockouts, payment failures) may need same-day handling outside the 3.

d0a254b5a85687d6d2dd4929.applies_when: Designing brand identity, packaging, creative direction, or new products where you're tempted to poll customers first.
conditions: This concerns the creative act; it is not a license to skip customer research, pricing tests, or post-launch data.
The presenter attributes this to Rubin and Jobs — treat as their philosophy, not a validated universal method.

59457b9fbb0937321aee4cf3.applies_when: Positioning a store in a crowded category where every brand sounds and looks the same.
conditions: Distinctiveness can narrow appeal; ensure the core offer still solves a clear customer problem.
Authenticity claims are the presenter's philosophy, not a measured conversion driver.

bfb0f531453be745217dbe1a.applies_when: Allocating effort between chasing metrics (views, follower counts) versus improving the actual product, photos, or content quality.
conditions: Obsession compounding is the presenter's analogy, not a linear formula with verified numbers.
The Mr. Beast and LinkedIn follower results are case examples, not promises.

9568b3b120a2034ff7f763e3.applies_when: Simplifying a cluttered PDP, navigation, product line, or ad concept that has too many competing messages.
conditions: Simplification can strip genuinely useful features; test whether customers still complete the task.
The Apple/Jobs story is illustrative, not a documented playbook you can copy directly.

64a076c5bf544df6d80b0488.applies_when: Deciding which organic channel to build for a store instead of posting thinly across X, LinkedIn, YouTube, and Instagram.
conditions: Single-platform focus trades reach for depth; revisit the choice only after sufficient reps.
The follower-growth example is a case result, not a repeatable promise.

6e16b5cd6b2ad46304009c0d.applies_when: Deciding whether to broaden a product line or deepen an existing category and internal standard of quality.
conditions: Depth can mean slower diversification; weigh against the realities of your category and cash flow.
The 'pain and suffering' language is the presenter's rhetorical framing, not an operating metric.

cb2126cc048b86240d26bb86.applies_when: You need a custom PDP, landing page, or storefront section (founder block, ingredient panel, size chart) that Shopify's default page builder sections cannot produce, and want it reusable across templates.
conditions: Sections live inside the theme, so changes are lost or overwritten if the theme is replaced or updated without carrying the file forward — keep a copy of the Liquid code outside Shopify.
Shopify's Edit Code interface labels and menu positions change; verify the current click path in your admin before following these steps literally.
Verify the section has valid theme-compatible schema and any preset needed for the Add Section picker; pasted HTML alone does not guarantee a configurable section.

3d2c297be2112e371f3c962e.applies_when: Merchandising a hero or specialty product on a bespoke PDP layout, or building a landing page where you want your custom section to render that product's data.
conditions: A custom product template only applies to products you assign to it; leaving a product on the default template means the custom layout will not appear.
If the custom section references product objects, it will render empty or broken on products that have no such data assigned.

9ffaac57744e0b85bdd0799b.applies_when: After adding a product through Products, Add product, before driving any traffic — you need to confirm the product is not showing as sold out or unavailable at checkout.
conditions: The 10,000 figure is just an example from the source, not a recommended stock level — set inventory to match your real replenishment plan.
Inventory can be tracked or untracked per variant; a product with inventory tracking on and zero available will display as sold out even if the page looks correct.

220bda0dd2e76d5a77002b6d.applies_when: Any time you complete a store setup task — theme code, product, payment, shipping profile or tax — before moving to the next setup item.
conditions: Preferences and interfaces vary; the specific test steps depend on your payment, shipping and tax configuration, so adapt the verification to each item.
Test orders and payment gateways may need test mode or refunding, which is outside the scope of the pure click path.

8818e8f9c5b2b51d4c4d2676.applies_when: You need to build a custom PDP section or page by hand in Shopify (no page builder), e.g. a branded product template for a new SKU.
conditions: Section code lives in the theme; theme updates or switching themes can drop or conflict with custom files.
Only edit code in a duplicated/published-safe theme if you cannot afford downtime.

54bad54781d139f87a424033.applies_when: You want one hero/paid-traffic product to have a unique PDP layout while all other products keep the default template.
conditions: Template names are arbitrary but must match what you assign in the product; mismatches silently fall back to the default template.
Hiding default sections is not deletion — you can restore them if the layout breaks.

d7c81282140d8c0a9cd5de68.applies_when: Immediately before driving paid traffic or launch content to a new product, to avoid wasting spend on an unbuyable PDP.
conditions: Setting a large inventory number on a drop-ship SKU does not guarantee fulfillment; keep it aligned with real supplier stock.
If you later toggle inventory tracking, re-check the PDP still allows purchase.

42a898b74a67918f501a193f.applies_when: Product selection: deciding whether to base a new store on a proven seller you found in ad libraries.
conditions: Scores combine one tool's ad-library data plus web research; without ad-library access expect materially less data (source cites roughly 55% of its data set).
Source opinion: a product can be validated yet still fail if you clone the incumbent instead of out-branding it.

7ff9026e43a5b88a5159b6cd.applies_when: Starting any reverse-engineering workflow (validation, branding, product mockup, page clone) and needing a clean source image of the target brand page.
conditions: Downloading a competitor's imagery is for research/inspiration; do not ship their copyrighted assets as your own.
Screenshots are reference inputs, not validated product data — pair with ad-library and store-level signals.

10d18b2b9c4aac5d1c230868.applies_when: Building a new store's brand from scratch when you already have a validated product and a competitor to model.
conditions: First-round AI names can miss the customer; plan to give corrective feedback rather than accepting the first list.
The source's chosen name and domain alternatives are examples, not recommendations for your category.

d3082ef30971df040a3986f1.applies_when: Preparing brand assets before sending a logo or packaging to a supplier or designer, or building landing-page visuals on-brand.
conditions: Generative image outputs are approximations — never send a generated logo to a supplier without recreating it precisely.
The source preferred one specific visual style/tool, which is a taste preference, not a universal rule.

26655e13ae5df22d87776555.applies_when: Briefing product mockup generation, a photographer/videographer, or a designer and needing one consistent description of what the brand stands for.
conditions: The guide is only useful if it is actually pasted into every asset workflow; a file nobody opens changes nothing.
Keep it descriptive and specific — generic adjectives produce generic imagery.

c962036d33a6f9bc46ef8a13.applies_when: Product sourcing and packaging prep: you need a visual target to send a supplier and to populate PDP imagery.
conditions: Suppliers can improve on your spec — treat it as a direction, not a final print file.
Generated mockups are concepts; verify dimensions and label legal/ingredient copy before production.

6fd1b113469847dfc4f95e94.applies_when: Building PDP, landing-page and ad creative imagery that looks on-brand without a photoshoot.
conditions: Output quality tracks prompt quality — the source states images are only as good as the prompts.
Reusing a competitor's exact composition may risk looking derivative; change props, setting and brand cues.

d175a55e416593dc6d1f1054.applies_when: Choosing fulfillment/sourcing model for a new store built around a validated product, especially when launch capital is limited.
conditions: The source's model sequence (dropship → ZenDrop/Spocket → private label) is a recommendation, not a proven mandatory path.
A branded PDP with an unbranded shipped product creates a visible mismatch — the source explicitly warns against this; reconcile imagery with what actually ships.

c386abd9ce999db19e031c79.applies_when: Building a homepage, collection page or PDP for a new brand when you have a proven competitor page to model and no page-builder available.
conditions: Tool names, plans and buttons in the source are vendor-specific and may change — verify the current interface.
Mirroring produces a neutral structural template; you still need to rebrand copy and imagery or the result reads as a clone.

40f69bed15d75cbb433a035c.applies_when: Pre-launch page review: improving a PDP or homepage before spending on acquisition.
conditions: The 55/100 figure and 'add all sections' advice are the source's tool and opinion, not a published standard — judge whether each section fits your offer.
Adding sections can lengthen the page; do not add a block that has no real content behind it.

005f75877ee9f35c260a4c15.applies_when: Auditing an existing product page or deciding which sections a new PDP needs before launch.
conditions: A high structural score does not guarantee sales; copy, offer, traffic and price still drive results.
Do not chase a perfect score at the expense of clarity or brand fit.

9229d200e653beccb176b4b2.applies_when: Deciding what content blocks to add to a product page that feels thin or isn't converting.
conditions: The exact mix should match the product's price point and buyer skepticism; not every section is mandatory for every SKU.
A guarantee must reflect a policy you will actually honour at scale.

3db5a6811648548ae9360168.applies_when: Generating product descriptions, benefit copy, FAQ text, or section headings for a new or refreshed product page.
conditions: Do not publish generated claims (health, efficacy, or timeframe) without verifying they match your product and comply with advertising rules.
More input improves output but never removes the need for human editing.

c7884fec6d58eb177a45a865.applies_when: Moving a page built in an external page designer into a live Shopify store.
conditions: Custom Liquid sections need maintenance when the theme updates.
Bundles and subscription options are configured separately in the product area, not inside the page section.

a8e85e602df89fd6dbe9a8fb.applies_when: Fixing or improving one block (e.g. a broken accordion) on an already-published PDP.
conditions: Placeholder-generated interactive elements (accordions, sliders) often need an explicit rebuild instruction to function.
Overwriting the wrong file or creating duplicates can break the page layout.

3dca4354b6dcee898443fb95.applies_when: Producing hero images, ingredient/lifestyle shots, and customer-use imagery for a product page or ad creative.
conditions: Generated images must be checked for accuracy against the real product — never show a product or result the customer won't receive.
Oversized uploads hurt layout and load time regardless of generator quality.

309fee9d852d8c26cdec17c5.applies_when: Deciding whether to build each PDP from scratch or reuse a section library for a multi-SKU store or a white-label brand launch.
conditions: Reusing one structure across many products can make a store feel generic if copy and imagery aren't genuinely differentiated.
The source's claim that the rebuilt page often looks better than the original is the presenter's opinion from a single build, not a measured result.

160e445095aef12015f257dc.applies_when: Planning a PDP for a new product where you lack your own conversion data.
conditions: Studying structure is not the same as copying copy or assets — produce your own.
A competitor's page may be optimised for a different traffic source and buyer awareness level.

9b0648a9c6841a962fbcafb7.applies_when: Finalising a new product listing before launching traffic to the PDP.
conditions: Inventory counts, currency and variant setup can override what the section displays; test an actual add-to-cart.
Bundles and subscriptions need separate app or platform configuration beyond the page section.

e5db2ba0cf5ec06c7520ed43.applies_when: Final QA pass on a PDP, landing page or store before running ads or sending traffic.
conditions: Incognito hides logged-in state and admin tools but won't simulate every device or slow connection.
Do a separate mobile check — the source demo was desktop-focused.

22f64fbbad91ec3509cd297c.applies_when: You want to make custom theme or product-page edits (new blocks, modified cart, custom templates) without hiring a developer or adding apps.
conditions: Install only the Anthropic-published extension among the many search results.
This sets up the tooling; it does not guarantee conversion improvements on its own.
Use an unpublished theme copy and preview changes before making them live.

cf190b41088d616c604142a7.applies_when: Your local Claude/VS Code environment is set up but not yet connected to your Shopify store, so you need it to see and pull themes.
conditions: Claude cannot authenticate on your behalf for security reasons; you complete login manually in the terminal.
Ask for the theme list first to confirm the connection before editing anything.

de00dc0259ba52881e03de68.applies_when: You are about to make any AI-driven theme change and need a safe staging environment.
conditions: Editing a live theme risks breaking the entire storefront if something goes wrong.
Do not skip the 'work only on that theme' instruction — otherwise Claude may target the wrong theme.

2068dc8e74a9d8f129581cee.applies_when: Your product page lacks shipping, guarantee and returns reassurance near the add-to-cart button and you want it editable without an app.
conditions: This is more capable than Shopify's Sidekick, which the presenter says can essentially only generate sections — Claude Code can add editable blocks and templates.
Build time in the example was roughly one to two minutes; longer prompts or many instructions can fail (see the one-change-at-a-time caveat).

100fb168dda1a3a70d8eb79c.applies_when: You want a structured, reusable PDP template beyond what your default theme ships with, and you already have a page anatomy/framework to follow.
conditions: The generated layout is a starting outline, not a finished page — expect to edit and remove redundant sections.
Don't assume the framework itself will translate into conversion gains without testing.

91ef75dc529d4c1732b48ab4.applies_when: You spot a specific high-performing UI element (e.g. a 'Top Seller' badge on a swatch) on a competitor's store and want an equivalent on your PDP.
conditions: Match the swatch label to the exact option value, or the badge won't bind to the variant.
Copy the styling pattern, not the competitor's trademark or content — avoid using their brand assets.
This copies a design element, not proven conversion results; test it on your own store.

5c660bd33ab3ce10a7cd37c5.applies_when: You want storewide cosmetic/UX changes (cart icon, cart count color, add-to-cart feedback) that aren't exposed as template-level settings.
conditions: The presenter's bundle of instructions produced the icons and colors but failed to implement the requested add-to-cart animation — too many instructions at once is the suggested cause.
If a requested feature doesn't appear, break it into a single focused follow-up prompt rather than assuming it worked.

9e2078f63db9660e4c99bf54.applies_when: You are planning a series of theme or PDP edits and deciding how to sequence prompts.
conditions: This is the presenter's observed lesson from a request that partially failed, not a hard rule — a clearly related bundle can still work but is riskier.

af0b1c6931028e1ee15c1e46.applies_when: You are doing multi-hour AI theme work and want to avoid running out mid-task.
conditions: The reset window (about an hour) and limit percentage are the source's observation and may change with Claude's plans — verify current limits.

35ef5d4ea699952de1dd3f0a.applies_when: Your AI-edited theme or template is validated and you are ready to push it live.
conditions: Publishing is the riskiest step — the source calls it the scariest part of the process.
Skipping the re-duplicate step means you could edit a stale copy and overwrite newer live changes.

16eefae8f3dd2f05d73eb0d6.applies_when: Setting up a brand-new WooCommerce store on Hostinger and needing a clean baseline before adding products, pages or shipping rules.
conditions: Menu labels and plugin bundles vary by host and WordPress version - verify the current admin interface before following click paths.
The 'Prima Sofas' title is an illustrative naming pattern, not a keyword recommendation for your niche.
This cleanup is for a fresh installation. On an existing store, use a backup and staging site and preserve cart, checkout, account, product and order data.

8c5a95292bdc4ce09575e115.applies_when: Adding products to a new WooCommerce store and choosing which product type template fits each item.
conditions: Variable products require attributes and generated variations; if you never generate variations the product shows no selectable options.
External/affiliate products leave your checkout entirely, so your payment, tax and shipping rules do not apply to them.

6a3060c2e498268447474f82.applies_when: Enabling payment collection on a new WooCommerce store and deciding where Apple Pay / Google Pay buttons show.
conditions: API key locations and toggle names change across plugin versions and provider dashboards - verify the current interface.
Express buttons appearing on product pages can create a separate checkout path that bypasses some cart logic; test both placements before committing.

a556c62817f0cb335d4f5222.applies_when: Choosing a landing page layout, template or redesign direction, especially when balancing brand creativity against conversion goals.
conditions: Jakob's Law is a UX heuristic, not a conversion guarantee; some strong brands convert well with differentiated design.

3f164438706e838967a8c214.applies_when: Auditing a landing page, collection page, PDP or cart to find why traffic isn't converting.
conditions: The five-step checklist is the presenter's own framework, not a validated universal method; treat each step as a hypothesis to test on your store.

bc8e0b03fd58bed4e5e3fc31.applies_when: Redesigning a store's top navigation menu or deciding where About, Blog and FAQ links belong.

af10d9d13cab03b6e3572747.applies_when: Deciding how many bundle or package tiers to show on a product page or offer page.
conditions: These lifts are one client case study with its own context; do not promise similar numbers or apply a fixed tier count without testing on your own traffic.

c8277a1ff908fb085f32b872.applies_when: Writing bundle and tier copy on a PDP or offer page where shoppers must compare options.
conditions: The 25%/28.5% figures are one client example; no universal effect size should be assumed.
