f5195fd1f7a66698d0e23cda.applies_when: A key team member wants to skip a planning session, launch review or pricing meeting for a customer or vendor meeting that conflicts.
conditions: Only credible if you actually have one clearly stated priority; the source's leader does.

ca4cfa68b414e8ecc7363e54.applies_when: Decide whether to pull merchandising, paid media and supply-chain leads out of trading for a planning reset.
conditions: Justification depends on dysfunction actually being the constraint; if the store's issue is a broken funnel or an out-of-stock crisis, time away has a higher opportunity cost.

49328275a84b048839a4addd.applies_when: Run weekly trading, range-review or campaign-planning meetings where people are half-attending and decisions stall.

acbe5b2bf41c1d77d87888ad.applies_when: Open an off-site or a first cross-functional planning session where the group is guarded toward each other.

d2ff2bd42550ba5eba32bb31.applies_when: Reduce friction between, say, a data-driven growth lead and an intuition-led brand lead before a joint planning cycle.
conditions: The source does not validate the instruments and one member dismisses the whole exercise as psychobabble; expect resistance and decide in advance how much to push.
Personality talk can become an excuse for behavior ('that's just how I am') if not tied back to results.

30921a836bb8c10fcc75ca5b.applies_when: A long-standing behavior (cynicism in reviews, passive-aggressive objections, chronic lateness) is souring a cross-functional team.
conditions: The source's own tension is that the leader wanted to protect the person being sniped at and chose not to; this is a judgment call about timing, not a rule to let conflict run unchecked.
Denial is a common response; escalation without a private follow-up can leave the person publicly cornered.

d16fde17aa021dd280f4daae.applies_when: Allocate your management attention across a team where some roles are ill-defined and some people are visibly disengaged.
conditions: The source's judgments of individuals are narrative setups in a fable, not validated assessments.
Tolerating an ill-defined role indefinitely carries risk; the source leaves it as an unresolved problem at this point in the story.

252c4066c43ebdc8558cf0c7.applies_when: Design incentives and the operating cadence for a merchandising, growth or supply-chain group whose members optimize their own metrics and never a joint outcome.
conditions: The source states the shift in reward systems as a recommendation with no data on outcomes; treat it as a design direction, not a proven incentive plan.
The specific meeting durations (two-day off-site, two hours weekly) come from one company's setup and may not transfer.

9e301567dac42327b7c7a44b.applies_when: When a store's weekly cross-functional meeting (merch, marketing, ops) keeps producing tense remarks or one person going silent during product or budget decisions.
conditions: All behavioral examples here come from the leadership fable; they are illustrations, not tested ecommerce findings.
Forcing vulnerability is explicitly shown to backfire when the person is not ready — the character Kathryn chooses not to force Mikey and later doubts that turnaround was possible.
The fable asserts that most people with that pattern never change ('for every one who did, ten never made it'); treat this as the source's opinion, not a rule for deciding who to fire.

25f1e4a02461ba32a008573c.applies_when: When setting or refreshing a store's team-level KPI dashboard so individual departments (merch, marketing, CX, ops) cannot pick self-serving metrics.
conditions: The seven categories are the fable's example for a software startup, not a validated ecommerce benchmark.
Existing metrics may be identical to the old ones; the fable's point is that the difference is using them collectively and on schedule, not the metric list itself.

ee63844c33b61def1f4e6617.applies_when: When store leaders say 'that's marketing's job' or 'that's fulfillment's problem' and no one intervenes cross-functionally to hit a quarter's goals.
conditions: Shared accountability is the book's prescription, not a measured result; expect resistance from strong individual performers.

In the fable, the CEO's blunt claim that the group was 'the most political' she'd seen triggered a defensive pile-on before it produced progress — delivery and follow-through matter as much as the message.

ec1ad28d6d5f3a920f7b166a.applies_when: When store meetings turn into departments lobbying for headcount, budget or shelf space, or when people avoid touching issues outside their own area.
conditions: The source warns that blurting a harsh verdict ('this is the most political group I've ever seen') can unite the team against the leader before the idea lands; deliver the diagnosis with a route to fix it.
If you haven't worked in the team's industry, expect the counterargument that your reference point is off; acknowledge it without withdrawing the substantive point.

95958a74d490f63498e135eb.applies_when: When a store's planning meetings avoid hard trade-offs (assortment cuts, discounting, outsourcing a process) and the same unresolved issue recurs every week.
conditions: The movie-versus-meeting comparison is the fable's rhetorical device; the actionable part is scheduling genuine decision debates, not an entertainment standard.
Conflict without a decision rule produces endless debate; pair this with a disagree-and-commit commitment step.

28c1fbbb868fdc20de0668b5.applies_when: When a merchandising, pricing or channel decision is announced and the team quietly under-executes because they never weighed in.
conditions: The source explicitly calls consensus 'horrible' when forced; this is the fable's strong opinion, so treat it as situational rather than a universal rule.
Disagree-and-commit depends on trust that dissent won't be punished; without it you get compliance with hidden resentment.

242e9d4d282d8fdff1b2c5bb.applies_when: When building trust in a new store leadership team, or when an offsite needs a concrete bonding exercise that feeds actual role decisions.
conditions: The source itself demonstrates failure modes: Mikey's five-second, note-reading answer was shallow and produced silence, and the leader did not force more — she judged that vulnerability has to come from the person.
A peer's joke at someone's expense during the exercise (as Mikey does to Martin) can wound and derail it; the leader in the fable later regrets not intervening.
Weaknesses disclosed are sensitive; treat them as real operating constraints, not ammunition in later reviews.

42e38198eea11eef134fa4fb.applies_when: When a store's leaders each champion a different priority (market share vs. product quality vs. cost containment) and the portfolio of initiatives dilutes focus.
conditions: The fable asserts that group egos tied to a clear score (winning) outperform individual-stats players, and shows a coach benching a talented stat-chaser who later credited that year as formative — an example, not a validated HR rule.
The source suggests that as more teams become collections of individuals, the advantage of genuinely team-oriented competitors grows; treat as a claim, not evidence about your market.

acd8b1cd9f28335536a69493.applies_when: When a store leader tolerates a peer's low standard (late launches, unanswered messages, missed handoffs) to avoid an awkward conversation.
conditions: The source frames accountability as executive-level and behaviorally difficult; it offers no measurement for how much peer confrontation is right.
Where hierarchical power is clear, the source notes people often already hold direct reports accountable — the gap is specifically the peer layer.

fcdcb7354b0cb7ad39cf3b31.applies_when: When a store only sees performance in income-statement or quarterly terms and can't change course inside the period.
conditions: This is the fable's operating rhythm, not a comparative study of review frequencies; monthly suited a startup's need for rapid feedback.
Weekly collection without group review is useless — the source contrasts weekly PR numbers nobody asked about with shared review that changes behavior.

a9b3f5dbd488f6613ed58cb5.applies_when: When a store leader delivers a hard diagnosis about team performance or culture and gets a defensive pile-on instead of engagement.
conditions: The source warns the leader's wording was probably too blunt, and the blunt version triggered a defensive alliance before the point landed — sequence and tone carry real cost.
This is a fable dialogue, not a communication protocol with tested outcomes; the mechanism (concede fairly, hold the substance) is the transferable part.

db956b04b10c5dc6f6ff1a99.applies_when: When rolling out a new process for a store team (planning cadence, performance reviews, reorg) and you meet open resistance rather than polite compliance.
conditions: The source is explicit that the painful heavy lifting is still ahead after the breakthrough conversation; don't mistake a good offsite for durable behavior change.
This is a leadership fable; the interpretation of resistance as a positive signal is the author's framing, not a measurement standard.

f89975959127e9b7af2211b2.applies_when: Setting the store's quarterly or annual priority — deciding whether to optimize for revenue, market share, new customers, repeat customers, or margin.
conditions: The source's specific figure (18 new customers, 10 references) is a fictional case illustration, not a benchmark.
A CEO unilaterally setting the number works when there is no data to decide; in a smaller store, the equivalent is that someone owns the call rather than averaging everyone's wishes.
Picking one goal does not cancel other goals — revenue goals still exist, they are simply not the ultimate measure this period.

5e46d0e232dde01447864b12.applies_when: Deciding what the next 90 days of store work is actually for — product range expansion, ad spend, SEO, retention — before allocating budget or headcount.
conditions: This is presented as a leadership stance in the source, not a universal law; businesses in maintenance mode or with a profitable core may legitimately run multiple balanced goals.
Choosing one goal privileges the stage of the business — an unproven store plausibly needs customers before it optimizes retention or margin.

bf4fc35fbd0f4ff2935f9499.applies_when: Scheduling a strategy offsite, brand workshop or planning day for an ecommerce team and deciding whether one session is enough.
conditions: The source presents this as a recurring pattern in leadership, not a measured average; the sequence is illustrative.
The 'one colleague wouldn't be around by the next session' prediction is a plot device, not a forecast method.

a5a2bf1b017e0831927ca5a2.applies_when: Investigating why store functions (merchandising, marketing, fulfillment, paid media) undermine each other, withhold information, or refuse to back company priorities over their own team's comfort.
conditions: Departments are not automatically wrong; the source keeps the point that departmental loyalty is valuable, it just cannot override company commitments.
For a small store where one person is both buyer and marketer, the 'first team' conflict takes a different form — usually founder versus contractor priorities rather than departmental turf.

78f85b7bed711deecdedfd3d.applies_when: Engineering a weekly or fortnightly ecommerce ops meeting that currently produces no decisions and no progress on the store's most important number.
conditions: The source's agenda sequence is a story illustration; adapt the number and driver list to the store's actual bottleneck.
Avoid exercising the process with no substance — the source deliberately replaces 'exercises' with real issues because abstractions produce polite agreement.

1255f54db7d347b5022228b4.applies_when: Fixing a store team that avoids challenging each other about slip, quality, or stalled work — e.g. late product photography, unvalidated ad spend, unshipped collections.
conditions: The line that every team member should push 'never hold back' is the source's prescription inside a committed leadership group; it is a cultural standard, not a license for public criticism of individuals who are absent.
Hard-to-hold-accountable people are categorized in the source as helpful, defensive or intimidating — treat that as an observation, not a diagnostic instrument.

26ec1e5e57818634657de823.applies_when: A store meeting breaks down — someone insults an absent colleague, mocks another function, or walks out mid-agenda — and the decision is whether to correct it now or later.
conditions: The source leader later admits she believed the person would quit — a public confrontation with a senior person carries real retention risk.

Correcting behavior in front of the group can itself become a morale event; the source uses the private option deliberately, except where the behavior was aimed at the leader and needed a visible response.

9cffbb518f9e472dfede2554.applies_when: A senior team member or key contractor in the store is agitating for a big new initiative, an acquisition, a second brand or a large hire mostly because they are bored.
conditions: The acquisition figures in the source are fictional case detail, not a template for evaluating real deals.
A big acquisition can still be right; the source's point is the sequence — resolve internal capability and politics first, then grow.

9df78b1b46854f8471a58ab5.applies_when: Diagnosing why your ecommerce leadership team (merchandising, growth, ops, supply chain) makes slow or reversed decisions before choosing an intervention like restructuring or new hires.
conditions: The scoring bands are the author's practical heuristics, not validated psychometrics; do not treat a 6 as a verdict.
Self-report scores can be gamed or unconsciously flattering; the conversation about discrepancies matters more than the number.

e77489155f5e30c3fd56114b.applies_when: Deciding where to invest management effort when your ecommerce team shows several problems at once (missed launch dates, silent meetings, finger-pointing between merchandising and fulfillment).
conditions: The model is the source's framework, not an empirically proven causal chain; treat ordering as a practical heuristic.
The source notes the behaviors are simple in theory but demand discipline and persistence that few teams sustain, so expect months, not weeks.

1fe3e28c3e6bf828f68e9943.applies_when: Assessing your ecommerce leadership or cross-functional team (e.g. growth, merchandising and supply chain) after a pattern of stalled decisions or unusual turnover.
conditions: The source's lists are practitioner observations, not a validated instrument.
Distrust is expensive in ways that are hard to measure directly (the source argues it consumes time and energy better spent on the work), so resist demands for a hard ROI before acting.

2221f16dc981ff7e49e48d61.applies_when: Evaluating why your ecommerce team avoids surfacing bad news about a failing SKU, a vendor delay, or a campaign that underperformed, even when individuals reliably deliver their assigned work.
conditions: The source stresses this is difficult and slow — vulnerability-based trust requires shared experience over time, repeated follow-through and understanding of individuals' unique attributes.
Distinguish carefully: reliability is still needed; the point is that it is insufficient for a cohesive team.

a50879793a42385ceeeb56f9.applies_when: Kicking off a newly formed ecommerce leadership team, integrating a new head of merchandising or supply chain, or restarting a burned-out cross-functional group after a bad quarter.
conditions: This is a first step, not a trust program; the source says vulnerability-based trust cannot be achieved overnight and requires shared experiences over time.
The author states these exercises must be paired with regular follow-up in daily work, or momentum is lost.

1c7756fd2d2111a7cb16d096.applies_when: When a team is functional enough to handle direct feedback but still has unspoken performance or behavior problems — for example, a merchandising lead whose dismissiveness is quietly degrading planning meetings.
conditions: The source acknowledges this is more rigorous and riskier than the personal histories exercise; it may feel intrusive and dangerous at first.
It assumes some baseline trust; the source notes even relatively dysfunctional teams can often make it work with surprisingly little tension, but results vary.

e3a83ce7c404d502569c1e09.applies_when: When recurring clashes between, say, a data-driven growth lead and an intuitive brand/creative lead are being read as personal conflict instead of stylistic difference.
conditions: The source notes many such tools require a licensed consultant, which it says matters to avoid misuse of their implications.
Profiles explain style, not competence; the author positions them as trust-building and conflict-handling aids, not performance verdicts.

59329495c17ebf3c1bda68d8.applies_when: Rolling out peer feedback across ecommerce functions (merchandising, marketing, ops) and deciding whether it will feed into reviews or salary decisions.
conditions: The author flags this as riskier than other trust tools because peers make specific judgments and deliver constructive criticism directly.
Without the firewall from compensation, the source expects the program to become political and lose its developmental value.

52a8c149b778a593e4373da5.applies_when: When you, as founder or ecommerce lead, want the team to surface bad news about a channel, a vendor, or an assortment bet earlier — but the team still filters what they tell you.
conditions: The source is a business fable-style treatment; the leader-first rule is a stated principle, not an experimentally verified threshold.
Exposure carries real risk in the short term — the author frames it as risking face so subordinates will take the same risk.

c873496d4cc03f3ce6227573.applies_when: Setting norms for how your ecommerce team debates pricing changes, discount depth, channel budget or a new bundle — before the next planning meeting.
conditions: The line between passionate debate and personal attack is often only clear in retrospect; the purpose test (best solution in the shortest time) is the source's proposed standard.
The source notes conflict is taboo at work and gets harder to permit the higher up the management chain you go, so norms must be actively maintained.

01b6d56e05d21cdb18c14a71.applies_when: Running an ecommerce planning or S&OP-style meeting where unresolved issues (inventory commitments, promo calendar, channel budget) keep resurfacing instead of being settled.
conditions: This takes courage and confidence from the person holding the role; in low-trust teams it can be read as aggression.
The source presents it as a technique for teams that tend to avoid conflict, not a universal meeting requirement.

620d53a81dad17e0956aa7b5.applies_when: Facilitating a contentious ecommerce decision — cutting a channel, changing a returns policy, repricing a hero SKU — and watching participants soften their position to reduce tension.
conditions: The source acknowledges it can sound paternal; it describes it as remarkably effective but not a fixed protocol.
Overprotective intervention is the specific failure mode the author warns against for leaders promoting healthy conflict.

dd193a22adc11bb8174f7b92.applies_when: When the same ecommerce peers repeatedly collide in the same way (e.g. one always yields on assortment calls, another always competes and forces a winner) and you want to change the pattern.
conditions: This addresses conflict style only; on its own it will not fix a trust deficit underneath.
The source treats it as a supporting tool, mentioning it in one paragraph rather than prescribing a full procedure.

40955f03802253cb4b2e9ecb.applies_when: A leadership meeting over the sales budget, headcount or channel investment turns tense and someone argues the team has regressed.
conditions: The source's example includes a direct clash between two executives that initially alarmed the rest of the team, illustrating that intensity alone is not a failure signal.
Do not use this framing to excuse personal attacks; the distinction between issue conflict and interpersonal conflict still applies.

d9382f94958b02b36874647d.applies_when: Right after an offsite or process reset, before the next quarter's numbers land — so the ecommerce team does not revert when channel performance and morale still look flat.
conditions: The source is a fable; the observation that the team laughed more and stayed together is anecdotal, not a measured benchmark.
Optimism should be tempered deliberately — the author has the leader 'let the air out of the balloon' precisely to avoid over-confidence.

35ddf3a597fadeceb1172914.applies_when: Handling a genuinely damaging team member — a merchandising or marketing lead whose dismissiveness is undermining peers — and deciding whether to attempt a turnaround or an exit.
conditions: This is a fable; the dialogue is illustrative and the specific severance and equity terms are not a template.
The source frames the leader's job as building a functioning team, not avoiding board confrontation, which is a strong stance stated by the character.
Candid feedback of the harshest kind (such as telling the person they seem bitter) is the character's choice, not a recommended universal script.

f9f956b15e91d0fc1674a65e.applies_when: Deciding whether to protect a top-performing ecommerce buyer, media buyer or engineer whose poor collaboration is driving colleagues out.
conditions: The story is a fable with a dramatic outcome; do not read the reported 50 percent productivity impact or the one-month recovery as measured benchmarks.
The source's lesson is specifically that manager tolerance is the causal factor, which may overstate the individual leader's role in complex team outcomes.

031f14e62d4992d3992befa0.applies_when: After terminating or losing a senior ecommerce leader, and noticing the leadership team's energy and meeting quality drop in the following days.
conditions: The story's device is a leader sharing a career failure; the specific narrative is illustrative, not a required script.
Mourning a difficult colleague's departure is described as nearly universal by the source, even when the person was the source of the problem.

eb9ccdf684874856d41a833e.applies_when: Managing the internal and external messaging after a senior ecommerce leader leaves — before employees hear it from someone else or a trade publication calls.
conditions: The source's example is a story; legal and disclosure obligations vary by jurisdiction and should involve counsel and HR.
The claim that employees 'won't be that surprised' is a character's expectation, not a measured outcome.

2ca0bcfdd550662f1929db6b.applies_when: Filling a senior ecommerce vacancy — head of marketing, merchandising or supply chain — when there is pressure to promote internally from the existing team.
conditions: The source's leader overrode a divided team; this is one situational choice, and the text does not establish that external hiring is generally better.
A public statement that no internal candidate is ready can damage morale; the source does not address that risk.

1cab46c8ddf756359dd1ca28.applies_when: Integrating a new senior hire — a marketing, supply chain or growth leader — into an established leadership team.
conditions: The source is a fable; the very quick integration described is illustrative and depends on the team already functioning well.
A new hire may find direct peer confrontation uncomfortable at first; the source shows that discomfort coexisting with enthusiasm to join.

0fde892e7e47cb30d51756de.applies_when: Your ecommerce company has grown past roughly a couple of hundred employees and the leadership meeting has become too large for fluid, substantive discussion.
conditions: The 'larger company, smaller top team' rule is the source's stated belief, not a measured threshold; the specific headcount and reporting structure come from the story's example.
Reducing direct reports can feel like a demotion; the source shows that peers will raise this concern, so address it explicitly.

a1fdc9095aecd3650801d4e4.applies_when: Team friction is slowing a merchandising, pricing, or vendor-negotiation decision, and the operator wants to help the team choose an appropriate conflict approach rather than defaulting to their habits.
conditions: The source presents the TKI as one helpful tool among several; it is not a prescriptive rule for every conflict.

68855d5d9f0249f75724e86a.applies_when: An operator is tempted to step into a merchandising or marketing disagreement between team members because they fear the conflict is becoming unproductive.
conditions: The source acknowledges this is difficult; the leader must still intervene if the team truly fails, but that should be a rare occurrence.

6b7f86825119bc9cae776b2a.applies_when: An operator is trying to get the whole team behind a product launch, pricing change, or campaign decision and is tempted to delay until everyone agrees.
conditions: This is the source's philosophy, not a universal rule; some decisions genuinely need more information, and the source still values research and analysis.

74974350d95811a330ae7d33.applies_when: A weekly or quarterly ecommerce team meeting is ending and decisions need to be communicated to store staff, vendors, or cross-functional partners.
conditions: The source says the exercise takes a minimum of 10 minutes; skipping it undermines the alignment it is meant to create.

f585db3667ae2d309ed04468.applies_when: An ecommerce team is stalling on a pricing decision, assortment change, or campaign launch and keeps revisiting the same debate.
conditions: Deadlines work only if they are actually honored; a deadline that slips without consequence reinforces the dysfunction.

9580c914ef466d7f3e908741.applies_when: A team is frozen on a high-stakes decision such as entering a new channel, launching a major product, or committing to a large marketing spend.
conditions: This is a fear-reduction tool, not a substitute for analysis; it is for teams that overvalue certainty, not for teams that routinely underanalyze decisions.

f6a0ee547b86f1545c085058.applies_when: An ecommerce team habitually delays decisions until exhaustive analysis is done, and the operator wants to build the muscle of deciding without perfect information.
conditions: The source explicitly says this is not a claim that research and analysis are unnecessary; teams with this dysfunction tend to overvalue them, which is the problem being corrected.

3c366caa7b8f140a66b6c2cf.applies_when: An operator leads a team that keeps deferring decisions and needs to set the tone that bold decisions with course-correction are acceptable.
conditions: The source frames this as the leader's responsibility more than any other member's, but it does not mean the leader decides everything; the point is to create conditions for commitment.

00e9c7d1cd6a0c4f66f49528.applies_when: An ecommerce team has performance or behavior problems and the operator is considering adding new policies or formal corrective processes.
conditions: This is the source's stated opinion that peer pressure is the most effective and efficient means; it is not a universal rule that formal performance management is never needed.

401b22a4cb2f0ce686a01da5.applies_when: An operator wants to make it easier for team members to hold each other accountable on a new initiative or across a cross-functional project.
conditions: The enemy of accountability is ambiguity; if goals and standards stay vague or private, peer accountability is much harder.

14e6bb26ffbb9ab1af3a90b0.applies_when: An ecommerce team is not giving each other feedback on performance, and the operator wants a lightweight review rhythm that surfaces problems early.
conditions: The source emphasizes structure, not heavy process; the goal is regular, simple reviews rather than a new bureaucratic system.

f865719ea5b40848a80933e6.applies_when: An operator is designing incentives for a store team — merchandising, marketing, fulfillment — and wants execution to depend on collective results rather than individual metrics alone.
conditions: The source notes that relying on rewards alone is problematic if it assumes financial motivation is the sole driver of behavior; team rewards are one tool among several.

e3909b2c8cdcde27ef712efe.applies_when: An operator finds that team members only raise problems to them, not to each other, and wants to shift accountability to the team.
conditions: The source warns that stepping in too often recreates the vacuum; stepping in too little risks the team never developing its own accountability.

3455fb9fc7e871775f6c1607.applies_when: An ecommerce team seems comfortable but is not hitting growth or profitability goals, or members are optimizing for their own function rather than the store's collective outcome.
conditions: The source's examples include nonprofits, political groups, and prestigious companies that fall into the status trap; the dysfunction is not limited to commercial teams.

b335017090014f73538ce8cc.applies_when: An operator wants a team or the whole store organization to raise its ambition and accountability around a growth or turnaround target.
conditions: The source notes that for athletic teams, public guarantees can unnecessarily provoke opponents; for most teams, public commitment is helpful. It is a motivational tool, not a guarantee of the outcome.

30d9d9379f9566c9b2b72094.applies_when: An operator is setting bonuses or recognition for a team and wants to avoid rewarding effort in the absence of results.
conditions: The source explicitly warns that relying on rewards alone is problematic; pair it with other practices.

d8ca93d60cfc514c4a1b754f.applies_when: An operator wants to build or repair a results-focused culture and is examining whether their own behavior is reinforcing or undermining it.
conditions: The source's claim is that the leader sets the tone more for this dysfunction than others; it does not mean the leader alone is responsible for results.

e7f4cb5fa94fd16f4b46b967.applies_when: An operator is deciding how much meeting time the management team needs and is weighing 'real work' against structured team time.
conditions: The source presents Kathryn's methods as one way to run a management team, not the only way; the numbers are a model, not a universal prescription.

79cb4207ec9548d50a9d074a.applies_when: Deciding your fulfilment model before registering an Amazon seller account or sourcing inventory.
conditions: Source is a single practitioner's preference, not a benchmark; FBM is not inherently worse.

a4f91430f890a0954f1f07d4.applies_when: Choosing which Amazon selling model to launch next quarter and how much capital to allocate.
conditions: Arbitrage and wholesale-specific sourcing metrics (BSR, seller counts, 30% ROI) do not transfer to private label or your own DTC store.
Capital figures are the presenter's stated examples, not guarantees.

f543c38ae44d63d19a5801ea.applies_when: Opening a new Amazon seller account in the UK and preparing for identity verification.
conditions: Specific fees and timelines are UK- and date-specific; verify the current sign-up interface and fees in Seller Central.

3f1b8c4c61475e58d0fd861c.applies_when: Preparing a newly approved seller account before adding your first ASIN.
conditions: The exact dashboard tasks and screens change; follow the current on-screen guidance.

2e113575bf73f95b1a097ba1.applies_when: Deciding whether to buy a specific branded ASIN for Amazon wholesale or arbitrage.
conditions: BSR and 30% ROI are this presenter's arbitrage/wholesale heuristics, not universal standards, and are not appropriate for private label or DTC.
Check gating/eligibility and current fee structures before buying.

394a2f9025bbb777515d51ba.applies_when: Judging whether a UK ASIN clears your profit threshold before committing to buy stock.
conditions: Contribution is not final net profit after all overhead.
Use the relevant marketplace and verified tax inputs; calculator estimates may omit some costs.

d00e98909a62d33950f44053.applies_when: Placing your first purchase order for a newly validated wholesale ASIN.
conditions: Test size is described as a range for beginners; some gated categories may require 10–100 units plus a supplier invoice to become eligible.

cee7349150a1e7c21d4aebc3.applies_when: Listing a validated wholesale or arbitrage product you are ready to sell on Amazon.
conditions: Gating thresholds and invoice requirements vary by category and brand; verify with Seller Central.
Sticking your own Amazon barcode over the manufacturer barcode is the source's commingling safeguard — this alters the physical unit, so confirm it does not conflict with the brand's requirements.

03f3588ec1844114cb3418d4.applies_when: Building a shipment plan to send stock from your premises into an Amazon fulfilment centre.
conditions: Source UK dimensions, label fees and carrier recommendations are historical examples, not current global requirements.

f2e93ddb9b519170f33fbab8.applies_when: Finalising an FBA shipment after confirming charges in Seller Central.
conditions: Carrier interfaces, offered time windows and templates change — verify the current UPS booking flow.
The drop-off vs collection choice affects cost and control; the source simply prefers collection for convenience.

680f24307e2ab558d2196eb2.applies_when: Screening candidate products for a new Amazon FBA listing before committing capital to inventory.
conditions: The $10 price floor and '$1/click' figure are illustrative from the source, not measured benchmarks.
Some sellers profitably run cheap or seasonal products; the source's guidance assumes a paid-PPC-led launch model.

78d7c95b14532e4f24b238d7.applies_when: Building the shortlist of products worth deeper keyword and competitor analysis for an Amazon launch.
conditions: 30% net margin and $25 minimum price are the source's heuristics, not industry standards; they vary by category and business model.
Low brand dominance is judged qualitatively — the source gives no numeric threshold for 'spread out' sales.

c7f835842a7659d4160fd222.applies_when: Deciding between two candidate products, or judging whether a niche offers cheap organic entry for a new Amazon listing.
conditions: The source gives no numeric minimum for 'enough' keywords — 'dozens' and '10/20/30/100' are illustrative.
Keyword counts and search volumes change over time; re-verify before committing.

aabcbafc75f4f712b66bf630.applies_when: Validating a candidate product's pricing power before sourcing inventory for an Amazon listing.
conditions: Prices on Page 1 shift with promotions, coupons, and seasonality; sample more than once.
Wide price spread does not guarantee you can occupy the high end — it signals room to try, not capacity to win.

c38799c1757bb3cdc3f8b752.applies_when: Running a first-pass product scan in Helium 10 Black Box (Products tab) to generate raw candidates for an Amazon FBA launch.
conditions: These are the presenter's personal heuristics, not proven thresholds; the source explicitly says not to follow the exact filters.

4f11afdcdf0d1d5801ab71ee.applies_when: Reviewing admin access, CMS/content tooling, plugin ecosystems, or any surface where store staff with elevated privileges view attacker-influenced content.

066cc7995ea405a87e2825d7.applies_when: Architecting a new storefront feature or reviewing an existing checkout/account flow where a single control currently stands between attacker and customer data.

014e55d2af7f379166751b76.applies_when: Hardening checkout, account, payment, or any one-click action page against having its buttons activated from another site.

047c9059541799ece3d14301.applies_when: Assessing your store's transport security, especially login, account, and browsing session cookies handled over shared or public networks.

96a63c6365a8aa7e735f9725.applies_when: Setting security strategy and expectations for an ecommerce platform — deciding how much risk to accept and where to invest, and explaining tradeoffs to stakeholders.

2630de3d9cca491c1186c780.applies_when: Designing or hardening customer account login, password reset, and high-value account actions on your store.

223a113427afb0f3343fdd66.applies_when: Auditing your storefront's privacy and third-party footprint — reviewing trackers, pixels, ad/analytics scripts, and what data leaves on page load.

The source gives no list of compliant tracker categories; consent and disclosure requirements vary by jurisdiction and are not covered here.

71f17dfd93083de74565474a.applies_when: Evaluating which storage and system APIs your storefront scripts use, and assessing risk from embedded or compromised third-party code.

1cda5fdc89c0207c90dca465.applies_when: Setting up a pentest, bug bounty, or internal security research program for an ecommerce site, or reviewing what staff and contractors are permitted to test.

2117b632489b5ee0dd1f55aa.applies_when: Hardening your storefront domain, or diagnosing why customers report landing on a look-alike checkout or phishing page for your brand, or selecting DNS providers and records.

b4d32aeac67fbdcc0dc24989.applies_when: Tuning caching/CDN rules, redirects and retry behavior for storefront and checkout endpoints, or diagnosing why a cached page or redirect misbehaves.

613eb3ed91ea2d79cec7bb79.applies_when: Operating a storefront behind a load balancer or proxy, setting timeouts and retry policy, or debugging intermittent checkout errors.

d721b7f8d72e454ee95976f7.applies_when: Evaluating whether path-scoped cookies protect a store's admin panel, embedded login, or a differently-scoped part of a site.

53a7573439dbefc02a7a1c66.applies_when: Designing credentials and permissions for ecommerce automations: price updates, inventory sync, order operations, customer-data access, marketing tool integrations.

ae9902b8b7a86ae8d4826cdc.applies_when: Designing defensive controls for high-value ecommerce operations such as placing orders, changing stored payment methods, issuing refunds, or editing admin permissions.

1b76024d8b1a18e44896bf5c.applies_when: Deciding the SameSite setting for storefront session cookies when your site relies on embedded widgets, affiliate links, email campaign links, or third-party checkout embeds.

The source's demo defense appeared to work once the attacker used a hostname rather than a raw IP, so test your specific deployment rather than assuming the browser will classify your attacker surface as cross-site.

conditions: Truncating a hash (as with hash prefixes) deliberately weakens it — collisions become expected, so a truncated match is a candidate, not a verdict.

c16f92a5d2c1b8d41ff4353f.applies_when: Threat-modeling your storefront or admin pages for what a third-party script or an embedded attacker page could infer about logged-in customers, cart state or history.
conditions: Most demonstrated attacks (reading QR codes via ambient-light sensor, recovering speech via gyroscope) are proof-of-concept and may be impractical in real conditions.
Fully eliminating side channels is not achievable; mitigations reduce precision or rate rather than guaranteeing elimination.

e336bbc883c66a3007e4a2b7.applies_when: Handling links to third-party or user-submitted destinations on product pages and deciding which link styling is safe to let influence layout or resource loading.
conditions: The source presents the 2010 browser mitigation as partial — later timing-based demonstrations still recovered visited history.
Some listed attacks require specific browser implementation details that may have changed; verify current behavior rather than assuming it still holds.

5f45b5443f6d7039425115fe.applies_when: Designing or reviewing any partner widgets, tracking pixels or third-party scripts that embed requests to your logged-in domains on a storefront or admin panel.

SameSite is the principal mitigation; without it, correctly implemented pages still leak login state.

353184970d3fd31f0283b30b.applies_when: Deciding whether to use device-sensor APIs (light, motion, orientation) in responsive storefront features and how to bound the risk of the data they expose.
conditions: The source notes these attacks are often impractical (full-screen, slow, visible) but were serious enough to make browsers reconsider shipping sensor APIs.
Sensor permission and precision behavior is browser- and OS-version-specific and changes; do not assume a current configuration.

d5c07946bb53959d1d013f60.applies_when: Building or reviewing any server-side feature that shells out — file viewers, image converters, PDF/CSV exporters, backup scripts — triggered by storefront or admin input.
conditions: The escaping function differs by language and framework; verify the safe API for your stack rather than assuming one exists.
Escaping arguments protects against shell metacharacter injection but does not make an arbitrary file viewer safe by itself — still restrict which files or operations are allowed.

79e6ed7e0b849cdf655473ba.applies_when: Reviewing how any user-supplied value reaches an interpreter (HTML, SQL, shell, template) on your storefront, checkout or admin tooling.
conditions: The correct escaping/parameterization mechanism is interpreter-specific; a fix for one context (e.g. HTML) does not protect another (e.g. SQL or shell).

f4b6df714ffd84d19fb5ed09.applies_when: You are building storefront features that shell out to a tool — image resizing, PDF generation, label printing, inventory export scripts, or any admin automation that runs a program on user-supplied values.
conditions: Escaping alone does not make an inherently dangerous command safe — the source explicitly notes that if the produced command is one you don't want to run, nothing protects you.
The source presentation is a classroom demonstration on a deliberately vulnerable app; do not test injection strings against third-party or production systems you do not own.
Argument-array APIs and their exact behavior differ across languages and versions; verify the current interface rather than assuming.
Do not claim that using argument arrays guarantees security — it removes one class of injection but not path traversal, authorization gaps or bad command design.

00899c6e9eb7ec7962209580.applies_when: You are reviewing or building store account login, order lookup, coupon validation, search filters, inventory reports or any admin query that embeds form input or URL parameters into SQL.
conditions: Single-quote testing is a diagnostic signal, not a proof of absence — a quote causing a different response suggests vulnerability, but a normal response does not by itself prove safety.

The source's examples are classroom demonstrations on an intentionally vulnerable bank app; do not run these strings against systems you do not own, and do not include working payload recipes in team documentation.
WAFs, input sanitizers or ORM usage do not by themselves guarantee safety; parameterization plus least-privilege database accounts is the durable control.
Verify current database driver and ORM behavior rather than assuming a specific API's protections.

976966f18f9b5137031d9349.applies_when: You are assessing the risk profile of a store search, filter, order-status lookup or API endpoint that returns a generic success/failure response, and deciding how much effort detection and parameterization deserve.
conditions: The timing values in the source are demonstration artifacts of a specific query on a specific machine, not a benchmark for detection thresholds.
Blind extraction is described as requiring creativity and patience; the source notes it is harder than visible-output injection, so prioritization should still weight visible-output endpoints higher.
Do not present error-page suppression or a WAF as a guarantee — both reduce signal for attackers but do not fix the underlying injection.
Time-based detection is noisy in real traffic; confirm before acting on alerts.

39c19437bd53e493457b92f6.applies_when: You are evaluating or implementing a link-safety or phishing-warning feature for a storefront — for example scanning user-submitted review links, affiliate URLs, supplier links or outbound links in marketing content before they are shown or clicked.
conditions: This is a blacklist approach and is guaranteed to miss cases — newly registered domains, unseen URLs with unique tokens such as private document links, and dynamic query parameters will not be listed. The source presents this as a trade-off: a whitelist would be unusable for the open web but may suit highly paranoid, narrow contexts.
Prefix truncation leaks some information: a provider can learn that you visited a URL matching a given prefix and could correlate requests over time by IP.
Always treat safe browsing as an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for browser protections or for your own link and content review.
List sources include user reports and automated crawling in sandboxed environments; coverage is not guaranteed and current behavior should be confirmed with the provider.

ec15a57caac841bbf3c653bb.applies_when: You are designing storefront or API logic that must not reveal whether a customer, coupon, account or inventory condition is true — for example email-enumeration checks in password reset, coupon validity endpoints, or stock lookups on a product page.
conditions: The source's vivid examples — recovering speech from high-speed video of a chip bag or plant leaves, and extracting keys from power-line monitoring — are research results in physical settings; they illustrate the general principle, not a threat model for an online store.
Do not present constant-time comparison, uniform error messages or rate limiting as a guarantee against all side channels; they remove specific observables.
Measurement-based validation on shared infrastructure is approximate and should not be treated as a certified threshold.

1a0f2ec23665c65763e44e76.applies_when: You are reviewing a storefront's CSS or third-party scripts embedded on PDP, checkout or content pages, and deciding whether any styling rule could reveal a visitor's prior browsing behavior to that page.
conditions: The source describes a 2010 change, attributed in the lecture to Mozilla/Firefox; browser behavior has evolved since, so treat the specific implementation as historical context and verify the current state.
This is a privacy leak of browsing history, not a data breach of your store's own records; the primary harm is to visitors.
Style restrictions do not make visited-link state invisible in principle — they reduce the channels through which it can be read.
Do not claim that removing a selector or a script guarantees no history disclosure, since other techniques may exist.

cda7d4680b56665b6fd1dc8c.applies_when: You are deploying an ecommerce automation agent that reads supplier pages, review content, uploaded CSVs, order notes or API responses and then acts — for example updating prices, drafting replies, creating orders or running scripts.
conditions: Do not claim that prompt filtering, a WAF or content sanitization alone guarantees safety against injected instructions in retrieved content.
Distinguish authorization from data handling: seeing a credential or an instruction is not permission to use it, and encryption protects data at rest or in transit, not the decision to act.
This card adapts the source's injection principle to agent inputs; the source does not present an agent-specific benchmark or outcome.

4b3b7d325f5f103fbe74e4d9.applies_when: Auditing storefront or marketing-site third-party scripts and ad pixels for the risk that they fingerprint visitors' browsing history, or advising engineering on what a page's own rendering performance reveals about customer behavior.
conditions: The timing technique is unreliable — the source's demo had false negatives (a visited link measured below threshold) though no false positives; enlarging the shadow was only a hypothesis for improvement.
This is a fundamental, hard-to-fully-fix client-side problem; there is no complete mitigation, so scope decisions to risk reduction, not elimination.
Do not assume any single browser mitigation (CSS whitelist, timing equalization, lying APIs) prevents all leaks — the source explicitly calls the solution incomplete.

a1ee46e37a85f0f8253c01a1.applies_when: Reviewing cookie attributes, third-party image embeds and account-state endpoints on a storefront, or threat-modeling how a competitor or attacker page could learn whether a customer is logged into your store or payment/email accounts.
conditions: There is no general way around the underlying information leak from image size/layout; SameSite cookies solve the cookie-attachment variant but not all size-based inference.
This is described as an unintentional leak violating the spirit of the same-origin policy, not a designed feature to rely on.
Exact browser cookie-default behavior is version- and vendor-dependent; confirm rather than assume.

5e21182dfef541f6aac2a9eb.applies_when: Deciding which browser sensor/permission APIs to allow or request on a storefront or PWA, or assessing privacy exposure of device-sensor features used for theming, games or interactive PDP experiences.
conditions: The demonstrated attacks are described as technically real but low-practicality (they occupy the screen and are visible to the user); practicality doesn't remove the policy violation.
Browser vendors were reconsidering whether to ship the ambient-light API unpermissioned — availability and protection status must be verified and may differ per browser.
Restricting these APIs also breaks legitimate demos and features; treat this as a security-vs-capability tradeoff, not a free win.

989b6ffaf61bca3a8c93eb92.applies_when: Deciding whether a storefront, web game or interactive product experience should request motion/orientation sensor access, and auditing which sensitive device-permission APIs your site invokes.
conditions: Locking down sensor APIs breaks legitimate orientation-based experiences; this is an explicit security-vs-capability tradeoff.
The eavesdropping demonstration was a research result, not a promise that arbitrary sites will succeed against modern devices — precision and OS gating affect feasibility.
Permission prompts do not fully solve the problem, because users may grant access for one purpose and the data may be used for another.

09f369da8351a62a5a65baf8.applies_when: Setting realistic security expectations for a storefront — deciding how much engineering effort to spend on browser-level hardening versus user education, monitoring and account controls.
conditions: Side channels are described as fundamentally hard, if not impossible, to fully prevent — plan for risk reduction, not elimination.
Phishing success depends on user behavior and cannot be fully engineered away.
Do not assume any single control guarantees security; treat each as one layer among several.

45a137425080896448130782.applies_when: Reviewing or writing any store backend code or admin/integration feature that shells out — file viewers, image/asset processing, export tools, report generators or third-party CLI wrappers.
conditions: Escaping input prevents adding commands to your program but does not prevent the program itself doing something dangerous with a valid-looking input (e.g. reading arbitrary files).
The source's live demo ran on the presenter's local interface only; do not reproduce injection tests against systems you don't own or have written authorization to test.
Exact function behavior (return value, escaping rules) is language- and version-specific — confirm against current docs.

bbfe8b258ef76bd9a226e897.applies_when: Reviewing authentication, search or account-lookup endpoints on a store for SQL injection, or testing whether an input field safely parameterizes queries.
conditions: No visible error does not prove a query is safe; code review and bounded validation are complementary.

478efa2d244c7f99603cbfec.applies_when: Choosing database query APIs for a store backend and reviewing existing endpoints that run SQL for login, logging or admin operations.
conditions: Protection against stacked queries depends on the API and database; a fix in one call path does not protect another.
The demonstrated password change and table drop are examples of impact, not guarantees that every injection yields them.
Do not test destructive payloads against systems you don't own or lack written authorization to test.

ef4261b02222d4f65c2d498f.applies_when: Assessing whether a store endpoint that accepts search/filter input and gives only success/failure or timing feedback could leak database contents, and prioritizing remediation for such endpoints.
conditions: Timing differences can have benign causes; confirm the root cause before declaring exploitation.

05ffb117c8363e8e47ee6558.applies_when: You are hardening checkout, login and account pages against network interception, and deciding an HSTS rollout plan for your storefront domain.
conditions: HSTS is effectively irreversible once cached by real users — there is no undo, which is why gradual max-age increases are recommended.
The first visit is still unprotected unless your domain is on the browser preload list.
HSTS state can be abused as a tracking/supercookie vector in third-party contexts; HTTPS and HSTS do not guarantee safety on their own.

3db5a465b9a7197e481a024d.applies_when: You are assessing third-party scripts, pixels or ad-network embeds on product and checkout pages for privacy and tracking exposure, or responding to a data-subject request to clear tracking state.
conditions: The source describes Apple/Safari and Chrome mitigations as evolving and states Chrome's plan was not final at the time; do not treat any specific vendor rule as a permanent guarantee.
Prevention is described as a trade-off between security and privacy, not a solved problem.

a8dbfcc8c9d3e8e8d08f7983.applies_when: You are deciding what security claims to make on your storefront landing page or checkout (badges, trust copy) and which protections to actually implement.
conditions: Positive security indicators such as lock icons were found by research cited in the source to be unreliable — users generally do not notice a missing indicator.
The source notes HTTPS adoption lagged in some regions historically and migrating large existing sites remains technically challenging.

302263a7609a37fd6dd69995.applies_when: You are setting up or reviewing domain-level certificate management for your storefront and want an implementable control against mis-issuance.
conditions: CAA does not stop a determined or compromised CA from mis-issuing.
CAs generally do adhere, but this is behavioral, not cryptographic enforcement.

214a75be3710ecab7f760e12.applies_when: You are evaluating whether to implement HPKP or certificate pinning on your storefront or deciding how to respond to pinning advice from a vendor or agency.
conditions: The source notes some operators were unhappy to lose pinning's safety benefits and were using hostile pinning as a feature; removal was a deliberate trade-off, not a claim pinning never helps.
Static preloaded pins still exist in Chrome for a curated set of high-value sites, but are not something a typical merchant can self-serve quickly.

982af2ed0756cc2ffa4e26fa.applies_when: You are deciding whether to submit your storefront domain to the HSTS preload list and how to sequence that decision.
conditions: The preload list was originally intended for a small set of high-value sites and grew into an unsustainable general list, per the source.
Verify the current preload submission and removal process, as the interface and policies may have changed.

896529f5c8fd1898c18ecac7.applies_when: You are migrating a legacy or large storefront to HTTPS/HSTS and need to sequence the rollout without breaking customers.
conditions: The specific timelines in the source are historical and may not match current browser behavior; verify against current documentation.
Not all environments can migrate at once — hosted platforms may enable HTTPS for you, while large custom deployments remain harder.

6d423be1f8d76318e8d22ea0.applies_when: You are auditing product, category and checkout templates for insecure subresource loads (images, scripts, fonts, pixels) and planning remediation.
conditions: Legitimate HTTP links will stop working, and the source acknowledges the change causes breakage.
Browser behavior around mixed content autoupgrading has evolved; verify current behavior in your target browsers before relying on it.

f25bc225d472e1e0b5319a23.applies_when: You are deciding how to communicate security to shoppers or being asked to approve a 'block by country/region' style control for your store or infrastructure.
conditions: The source's remarks on certificate authorities and geography are situated in web-PKI context; regional or IP blocking can still have legitimate, non-security uses such as regulatory controls.
This is a strong opinion from the presenter, supported with historical examples rather than a controlled study.

de68d498e43178c1ae0baeb2.applies_when: You are specifying security requirements for storefront accounts, payment integrations, agent credentials or admin access and need to state each control precisely.
conditions: The source's specifics about SHA-256 pinning and HPKP describe a deprecated mechanism; the general distinction between key pinning and certificate/serial pinning remains valid.
Current algorithm and protocol guidance changes; verify against current standards before implementing.

8af1481061ca80b5ef911906.applies_when: You are building or reviewing an ecommerce agent that reads supplier documents, product feeds, customer messages or web pages and can then call tools like price updates, refunds or order changes.

Verify the current capabilities and limits of whichever agent framework you deploy against current vendor documentation.

39365bbd8ce0ad86a5be8b32.applies_when: You are validating a suspected weakness (timing side channel, credential stuffing, insecure subresource, injection) in your own storefront before remediation.
conditions: Testing systems you do not own or are not authorized to test is out of scope and potentially unlawful.
A timing difference observed on your environment may not reproduce on production due to caching, load balancing and network variance.

380c74d6b66f5aa5d8d711d7.applies_when: You are threat-modeling domain impersonation of your storefront (phishing clones, fake checkout pages) and choosing which certificate controls to deploy.

191bf7e72dfe1dc4b1e158ae.applies_when: You are pushing an HTTPS/HSTS or mixed-content cleanup across a large store or multi-brand ecommerce organization with legacy systems.
conditions: The source's remarks on adoption levels and regional patterns are historical observations, not current benchmarks.
Specific performance claims about modern protocols should be verified in your own environment before being used as a business case.

ee326648c4322bce58ad9c8f.applies_when: You are selecting a certificate-issuance strategy or vendor for your store and weighing convenience against assurance.
conditions: The source presents pinning removal as a deliberate trade-off, noting that pinning works when everything is aligned.
Static preload pinning still exists for a curated set of high-value sites; eligibility and process are not self-serve.

46771a8e61d2b9d86cc0fb5b.applies_when: Deciding how to monitor for fraudulent or mistakenly issued TLS certificates on your store's customer-facing domains.

d63cc78167711c7d616f01ad.applies_when: Designing login, session, and admin-role handling for a storefront or its backend (customer accounts, staff/admin panels).
conditions: The source presents this as general guidance; exact mechanisms (ACL vs capability tokens) trade off revocation and simplicity.

9b569cd2522a5a66a8a9ecac.applies_when: Implementing customer account creation and login for a storefront where usernames or display handles are used.

81c60e09127fead56af1c0dc.applies_when: Setting password rules for your store's customer accounts or admin logins.

f753de594e4c840934919fab.applies_when: Hardening the login endpoint of a storefront or admin panel against automated credential guessing.

115d25c9c19dd9100fe18f12.applies_when: Deciding how much to rely on CAPTCHA to protect signup, login, or high-abuse store actions (e.g., promo-code redemption, inventory hoarding).
conditions: CAPTCHA vendors and solvers evolve; verify current effectiveness rather than assuming these figures still hold.

813fb79b2bef6ba017be332b.applies_when: Choosing minimum password length and hash settings for customer or admin accounts based on how exposed your credential database is.
conditions: The source presents crack-time figures as illustrative assumptions about guessing rates and hardware, not fixed benchmarks.

a55298b2b401168a38fd013c.applies_when: Deciding which authentication factors to offer for customer logins and which to require for admin/staff or high-value store actions (e.g., payouts, price changes).

b6d76d1c801a7aa030114372.applies_when: Evaluating whether any trust badge, security image, or pre-login indicator on your storefront actually protects customers from phishing lookalikes.
conditions: The source describes these indicators as deprecated and ineffective, acknowledging they may once have helped; effectiveness studies are dated relative to current phishing tooling.

7234ed15210a15b1bb4abdd0.applies_when: Deciding how strict login policy should be for different account tiers in a store (casual shopper accounts vs. accounts with stored payment, payout, or admin access).
conditions: The source's examples of account sensitivity (streaming vs. financial) are its own illustrations, not measured outcomes for any named service.

103d992322b16d85fe847aa4.applies_when: Architecting login and account protection for a storefront where credentials commonly leak or get reused across sites.
conditions: The source gives this as a design principle, not a specific product recommendation; pick concrete controls that match your stack and sensitivity.

b6026850aadfd2803617fc1c.applies_when: Deciding how much to rely on CAPTCHA/reCAPTCHA to protect storefront login, account creation, checkout, or admin actions.
conditions: Solver success rates quoted in the lecture are examples from a specific set of schemes and years, not current benchmarks for any vendor. Verify current vendor and third-party assessments before choosing a scheme.

00647bf08fc4765bf8cf8a72.applies_when: Choosing or configuring a bot-mitigation service for login, account creation, checkout, or coupon/inventory abuse on your storefront.
conditions: The lecture describes the general mechanism, not any specific current product. The exact signals, APIs, and no-UI behavior must be verified against the vendor's current documentation.
Cross-site reputation inherently penalizes some legitimate users and introduces dependence on a third party seeing your traffic.

930806e85a10566c5dfa27e4.applies_when: Designing the admin/customer account flows where you allow changes to saved payment methods, shipping addresses, email/password, or payout/account details.
conditions: The source is explicit that this is 'not perfect' and does not cover every action — it is defense-in-depth, not a replacement for fixing XSS/CSRF or for MFA.
Adding re-auth adds friction; scope it narrowly to actions whose compromise is genuinely costly.

83bd8b5f52f4104b9a8e394c.applies_when: Writing the copy, logic, and status codes for storefront login, signup, guest-checkout account detection, and password-reset forms.

Generic messages must be applied to every related flow or the fix is incomplete.

d3e7e7ef57eb65fb90b4ec5c.applies_when: Reviewing or writing login/password-check code where a database or service call only happens when the user exists.
conditions: The source itself admits it does not know how to guarantee a remote database takes identical time; treat timing mitigation as best-effort and validate.
Timing differences are only one of several enumeration channels (messages and status codes leak state more easily).

a84a0c3caf46c6aeb24826a2.applies_when: Setting thresholds and locking policies for storefront login, password reset, and signup endpoints.
conditions: The 'order of magnitude above the extreme user' guidance is the source's personal rule of thumb, not a calibrated benchmark; you must test against your own traffic.

e67276b1419526dda886eade.applies_when: Choosing and enforcing password policy at account creation and password change on your storefront.
conditions: This doesn't stop an attacker who already has a valid password; pair with MFA and rate limiting.
Breach coverage is imperfect — absence from a list is not proof the password is safe.

fe3628d7cc6565a71f6c10a9.applies_when: Incident response and ongoing account hygiene for a storefront whose customers reuse passwords across sites.
conditions: Proactive locking creates friction and support load; scope it to accounts actually confirmed in a breach rather than guessing.
You will not have visibility into all breaches affecting your customers.

9d8f903b4f271438bec07e23.applies_when: Designing or auditing how your storefront stores customer and admin credentials.
conditions: Algorithm requirements can differ by platform or compliance context. Password hashing does not stop credential reuse, phishing or a compromised login endpoint.

385b678a734e6f03b9276d0f.applies_when: Deciding whether to require MFA on your storefront and explaining the value to stakeholders.
conditions: The source's framing ('passwords are broken', choose anything) is deliberately stark and comes from the cited Microsoft blog post — treat it as an argument for MFA, not a claim that password hygiene is pointless if MFA isn't available.

75c876a254f308972ef7c86a.applies_when: Designing when to add an MFA prompt in storefront login and account flows without hurting conversion.
conditions: The lecture's IP and volume thresholds are examples, not calibrated controls for the store.

1ce56e83712a4b2a98a8176b.applies_when: Choosing and implementing a second factor (TOTP/hardware key) for storefront customer and admin accounts.
conditions: The shared secret stored on the phone and server is sensitive; losing the device means losing the factor, so provide recovery codes or a second enrolled factor.

cb2bba93c89db68e9c998706.applies_when: Planning a passwordless or hardware-second-factor login option for customer and admin accounts on your storefront.
conditions: WebAuthn shifts trust to the device vendor and platform; it does not eliminate all account-recovery risk.
Passwordless isn't a universal fit — many users lack a suitable device or password manager, so the source treats it as an alternative rather than a replacement for everyone.
The source's discussion of factor categories is explicitly framed as a design abstraction, noting that not all authentication mechanisms fit neatly into know/have/are.

c7048790c8bc922cc41bb2c4.applies_when: Designing account recovery and verification for storefront customer accounts, billing support, and admin access.
conditions: The source's factor framework is presented as an abstraction that shouldn't be rigidly applied — you ultimately care about keeping the attacker out, not whether a mechanism matches a category.
Some users will not have modern device factors; provide a fallback path that is still stronger than a security question.

a92370ed045d706ca33078d4.applies_when: Reviewing your store's storage buckets, servers, and database access for accidental public exposure.
conditions: This is a general reminder, not a complete audit checklist — many breach causes are out of scope of the source.
Assume your customers reuse passwords elsewhere, so even a non-financial breach on your store can enable attacks on other services.

d6e5ce45fe0b0398b10efb14.applies_when: Standing up account-security review processes for a storefront, and checking your team's admin/ops accounts for exposure.
conditions: Do not expose or log checked passwords; use a k-anonymity/bulk-check approach and verify the current API's privacy model.
The source's 'four random words' advice is offered as an approach, not a formal benchmark.

8a2882319f8c9f3c68670db7.applies_when: Deciding what login and account-recovery methods your storefront should accept, or auditing why a 'two-factor' customer account can still be taken over.
conditions: The source is a technical talk on authentication, not a study of storefront conversion impact; treat usability trade-offs as judgment calls to test, not measured results.
Carrier number-reassignment policy is jurisdiction- and time-specific; verify current practice before relying on SMS as a sole recovery path.

be571a894d84534268762622.applies_when: Designing or reviewing the forgot-password, magic-link login, or email-verification flow on a storefront.
conditions: Requiring hardware keys for all consumer shoppers will cost conversions; scope strict controls to privileged or high-value accounts unless you can measure the trade-off.
Email provider security varies; the source's claim that a link equals full account access depends on whether additional factors are required.

c16584de911d24b158ff295e.applies_when: Reviewing branded or in-house authentication schemes on your site, or a vendor pitching a custom 'trust indicator' before login.
conditions: The source dates this to pre-HTTPS-era banking practice; current browsers and standards may handle these cases differently, so verify what your stack actually does.
This card addresses server-impersonation defenses; it does not cover how to detect account takeover after login.
